9. 
PROPOSED VEHICULAR AND PEDESTRIAN TRAFFIC 
CIRCULATION: 
 
Traffic Circulation: 
 
Currently, the 495 Project Site has access from Dorchester Avenue and Alger Street. 
Alger Street will be improved, as will the sidewalks on Dorchester Ave. 
 
 
Pedestrian Circulation: 
 
The new sidewalks will be constructed to be in compliance with the City of Boston 
Complete Streets guidelines, with trees, landscaping, crosswalks, signage and other pedestrian 
friendly facilities. The major pedestrian routes will be along Dorchester Avenue, Alger Street, 
and the future Ellery Street. The MBTA Andrew Square Red Line T stop is approximately 150 
feet to the south of the 495 Project Site and pedestrians will be able to easily access this major 
subway and bus facility from the 495 Project Site. 
 
 
10. 
PARKING AND LOADING FACILITIES: 
 
Parking facilities will be provided underground, beneath the building with a total of 
approximately 88 underground parking spaces. The loading areas for the 495 Project will be off 
Alger Street and the below-grade parking garage entrance will be off Alger Street. The garage 
parking spaces included in the 495 Project need not comply with any parking stall or 
maneuvering aisle dimensional requirements of the Code. 
 
 
The 495 Project’s parking and loading facilities shall be subject to review and approval 
by the BPDA in accordance with the requirements of Article 80. Upon the issuance by the 
BPDA of a Certification of Compliance and a Certification of Consistency (or Partial 
Certification of Compliance or Partial Certification of Consistency, if applicable), the parking 
and loading facilities for the 495 Project and for each component of the 495 Project shall be 

 
 
 
deemed to be in compliance with the requirements of the Restricted Parking Overlay District and 
all other parking and loading requirements set forth in the Code. 
 
11. 
ACCESS TO PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION: The 495 Project Site is located 
within convenient distance of the MBTA public transportation system. The Red Line Andrew 
Square Station is located to the south, at a 3-5 minute walking distance from the 495 Project Site. 
Andrew Square Station is also a major MBTA bus hub. Many bus routes go through the station 
and make regular stops along Dorchester Avenue. 
 
12. 
ARTICLE 80B, LARGE PROJECT REVIEW: The undertaking of the 
Development (including without limitation the 495 Project) has been subject to Large Project 
Review by the Authority. In accordance with the requirements set forth in Section 80B, the 
Developer caused to be filed a Project Notification Form for the Project dated June 10, 2021. On 
March 16, 2022, the Developer filed a Draft Project Impact Report, and a Supplemental 
Information filing was made on June 30, 2023. 
 
13. 
AFFORDABLE HOUSING: The 495 Project includes 331 housing units, of 
which 94 units will be used for affordable housing serving low and very low-income seniors, 
with significant amenities and supportive services, dedicated to enhancing resident quality of life 
and maintain independent living as the residents age. These units represent 28% of the units of 
the 495 Project, well in excess of the City of Boston Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”) 
requirements, and the requirements of the PDA Master Plan. 
 
The 495 Project will also be fully compliant with the City of Boston Affirmatively 
Furthering Fair Housing and Affirmatively Integrated Communities (“AFFH”) policies and 
requirements. The Developer has been working with the Boston Interagency Fair Housing 
Development Committee (“BIFDC”) on the AFFH policies and requirements and will continue 
to work with BIFDC during the ongoing review process for the 495 Project. 
 
 
14. 
PUBLIC BENEFITS: The 495 Project, as a part of the Development, will 
provide substantial public benefits to the City of Boston and the surrounding neighborhood. 
These benefits will include: 
 
 
• Provides much needed housing and elderly housing in South Boston. 
 
• Provide service enriched senior housing with programming and supportive services 
provided for elderly residents to maintain independent living while aging in place. 
 
• Increase the availability of high quality housing stock in addition to furthering IDP and 
AFFH goals and requirements. 
 
• Provide that the issuance of a certificate of occupancy for the residential units at 495 
Dorchester Avenue occur prior to the issuance of any certificate of occupancy for any 
non-residential building included as part of the Project, ensuring that residents are 
present to help activate the portion of the 495 Project Site along Dorchester Avenue. 

 
 
 
 
• Provide for linkage funding from remainder of Phase 1 of Master Plan PDA (i.e., Phase 
1B) to be used for assistance with the financing for the construction of the 495 Project, to 
be further provided for in the PDA Development Plan for such phase. 
 
• The 495 Project transforms a contaminated former industrial site to create a safe, 
multimodal district through robust pedestrian, bicycle, and vehicle infrastructure that 
complies with Complete Street guidelines. 
 
• Improves pedestrian safety with new wider sidewalks, crosswalks, curbs, bike lanes and 
street trees along Dorchester Avenue and Alger Street to comply with Complete Streets 
guidelines. 
 
• Leverages existing nearby transit and alternative transportation choices to establish a 
true, transit oriented, development. 
 
• Targets LEED Platinum, all-electric, and Passive House standards to foster 
sustainability. 
 
• Improves resiliency by raising 495 Project Site grades and complying with flood district 
requirements. 
 
• Enables extensive environmental stabilization and remediation of land that was utilized 
for decades as a metal scrap yard that is currently under regulatory oversight by the 
federal EPA and Mass. DEP. 
 
• Identifies ground floor active retail space to be subsidized for the build-out and ongoing 
operation costs and made available to community start-ups, artists needing maker and 
industrial arts workspaces, and similarly identified community groups and programming, 
in conformance with the goals of the BPDA PLAN: Dot Ave. 
 
• Greatly improve stormwater and sewer infrastructure. 
 
 
15. 
DEVELOPMENT REVIEW PROCEDURES: All design plans for the 495 
Project are subject to the on-going development review and approval of the Authority. Such 
review is to be conducted in accordance with Article 80 of the Code and the Authority’s 
Development Review Procedures, as they may from time to time be updated. Once this 
Development Plan is approved, the BPDA may approve changes to the plans for the 495 Project 
without the need for an amendment to this Development Plan as part of its development review 
and approval. 
 
16. 
COASTAL FLOOD RESILIENCE OVERLAY DISTRICT: Portions of the 
495 Project Site along Alger Street are within the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District 
(“CFROD”) and are subject to the requirements of Article 25A of the Code. The portions of the 

 
 
 
495 Project Site governed by the requirements of the CFROD have been designed to comply 
with said requirements. 
 
 
17. 
CONSISTENCY WITH THE PDA MASTER PLAN: This Project described 
in this Development Plan is consistent with the overall planning objectives and character of the 
Development described in the PDA Master Plan. The dimensional provisions, allowed uses, 
landscape phasing, parking and loading provisions described in this Development Plan shall be 
controlling for the Project and are consistent with and in compliance with the provisions in PDA 
Master Plan No. 144. 
 
 
18. 
APPLICABILITY OF ZONING CODE: Upon the approval of this 
Development Plan, in the event that the 495 Project (or any portion of the Project) described 
herein conflicts with any provision of the Code, such requirements of the Code shall be deemed 
waived. In accordance with the provisions of Section 80C of the Code, the BPDA shall be 
required to issue a Certification of Consistency (or partial Certification of Consistency) for the 
Project or portion(s) thereof. Upon the issuance of a Certification of Consistency (or Partial 
Certification of Consistency, if applicable) such Project or portion thereof shall be deemed to 
comply with any use, dimensional or other requirements of the Code. 
 
19. 
OWNERSHIP OF PROJECT SITE AND PROJECT. Although the 495 
Project Site is currently a portion of a single lot, it is contemplated that the 495 Project may be 
separately owned and financed including, without limitation, by the creation of separate parcels, 
condominium ownership, ground leases, or otherwise. The compliance or non-compliance of 
any other project described in the PDA Master Plan shall not affect the compliance of the 495 
Project with the requirements of this Development Plan. The Project will be eligible to receive 
its own Certification of Consistency or Partial Certification of Consistency if, and only if, the 
Director of the Authority makes the findings set forth in Article 80C-8 of the Code. If the 
Project is separately owned, the owner of the Project may seek an amendment of this 
Development Plan as to the 495 Project, provided that such amendment does not change any 
obligation or requirement of the PDA Master Plan, or any other project built in accordance with 
a separate development plan pursuant to the PDA Master Plan. 
 
20. 
LIMITED UNDERTAKING: Nothing in this Development Plan shall be 
construed as an undertaking by the Developer to construct or complete the 495 Project. 
Notwithstanding the fact that (i) the 495 Project is described in the PDA Master Plan and in the 
Article 80B Documents (as hereinafter defined), each of which describe the construction and use 
of the Development and all of the Proposed Projects, and the mitigation of the impacts from such 
construction and use; and (ii) the construction and operation of the 495 Project is authorized 
under the Code pursuant to the PDA Master Plan and the Article 80B Documents, the sole 
obligation of the Developer under this Development Plan, is to adhere to the provisions of this 
Development Plan, the PDA Master Plan, and the Article 80B Documents applicable to the 495 
Project. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, upon approval of this Development 
Plan for the 495 Project, the Developer hereunder shall not be chargeable with any omission, 
commission, default or delay by any other person, including without limitation the developers of 
any other Proposed Project, in the implementation of the PDA Master Plan, or any other 
approved Development Plan, or the undertakings of the Article 80B Documents with respect to 

 
 
 
any other Proposed Project or any other portion of the Development. This provision to make the 
undertakings with respect to each Proposed Project severable is included in order to facilitate the 
separate ownership and/or financing of portions of any Project without concern for any so-called 
cross-default or zoning non-compliance attributable to the acts of others.

1. 
PLANNED DEVELOPMENT AREA DEVELOPMENT PLAN: On October 
12, 2023, the Boston Redevelopment Authority, doing business as the Boston Planning & 
Development Agency (the “Authority”) approved the Master Plan for Planned Development 
Area No. 144 (the “PDA Master Plan”) pursuant to Article 3, Section 3-1A and Article 80, 
Section 80C of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”) for the parcels of land along Dorchester 
Avenue in South Boston (the “Development”). Capitalized terms used herein without definition 
which are defined in the PDA Master Plan shall have the meanings ascribed to them therein. 
 
On December 13, 2023, the Boston Zoning Commission (the “Commission”), by the 
adoption of Map Amendment No. ____, approved the PDA Master Plan and amended the series 
of maps entitled “Zoning Districts City of Boston,” dated August 15, 1962, as amended, by 
adding a “D” designation, indicating a Planned Development Area overlay district, to the Project 
Site. 
 
In accordance with Article 3, Section 3-1A of the Code and Article 80, Section 80C, this 
development plan (the “Development Plan”) sets forth information on the construction of Phase 
1B of the Development comprising (a) three (3) new buildings to be located at 65 Ellery Street, 
75 Ellery Street and 505 Dorchester Avenue; (b) two (2) new open space areas to be located 
between 65 Ellery Street and 75 Ellery Street (West Open Space), and between 495 Dorchester 
Avenue and 505 Dorchester Avenue (East Open Space); (c) construction of three new streets - 
Ellery Street, Service Drive and a street referred to as “Street A” until a more permanent name 
can be established, along with improvements to Dorchester Avenue and Alger Streets (the 
“Project”). The Project is located on an approximately 343,820 sf portion (the “Project Site”) 
of the of the approximately 21-acre site described in the PDA Master Plan along Dorchester 

 
 
 
 
Avenue in the South Boston section of Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts. The Project Site 
is currently vacant. It has long been used for industrial purposes and the Project will entail 
substantial environmental remediation due to the prior industrial uses. 
 
The PDA Master Plan contemplates that one or more PDA Development Plans for phases 
of the Development may be submitted either simultaneously with or subsequent to the 
submission of the PDA Master Plan. The Development Plan for 495 Dorchester Avenue (Phase 
1A) was approved by the Authority on January 18, 2024. This Development Plan comprises the 
remainder of Phase 1 as described in the PDA Master Plan. 
 
This Development Plan includes the proposed location and appearance of structures, open 
spaces and landscaping, the proposed uses of the Project, the proposed dimensions of the 
structures, the proposed densities, the proposed traffic circulation, parking and loading facilities, 
access to public transportation and other major elements of the Project. This Development Plan 
constitutes the permanent zoning for the Project and supersedes any existing zoning requirements 
contained in the Code. 
 
 
2. 
DEVELOPER: The owners and developer of the Project Site is On the Dot LLC 
and entities affiliated with Core Investments, Inc. (with their successors and assigns, the 
“Owner” or the “Developer”). 
 
3. 
LOCATION AND DESCRIPTION OF THE PROJECT SITE: The Project 
Site is the approximately 343,820 square foot portion of the land described as Phase 1B and Phase 
1C in the PDA Master Plan. As of the date of this Development Plan, the Project Site has not been 
subdivided into separate lots for zoning purposes. The Developer shall have the right to so 
subdivide the Project Site at any time, which subdivision shall not require amendment of this 
Development Plan. 
 
The Project Site lies in the South Boston District and more particularly within the I-2 zoning 
district in which Planned Development Areas are allowed (the “Zoning District”). 
 
4. 
PROPOSED LOCATION AND APPEARANCE OF STRUCTURES: The 
Project consists entirely of new construction elements and the following are the dimensions of 
each new structure: 
 
65 Ellery Street: Proposed as a 13-story, 217-foot tall (including mechanical penthouse 
and screens), 510,900 GFA sf mixed use laboratory, research & development, office, and retail 
building, including up to 604 vehicle parking spaces (valet) or up to 484 vehicle parking spaces 
(non-valet) and 202 bicycle parking spaces in a three (3) level below grade parking structure. 
 
75 Ellery Street: Proposed as a 13-story, 217-foot tall (including mechanical penthouse 
and screens), 388,200 GFA sf mixed use laboratory, research & development, office, and retail 
building, including up to 169 vehicle parking spaces and 152 bicycle parking spaces in a two (2) 
level below grade parking structure. Sixty-four (64) of the 152 bicycle parking spaces are 
provided to serve the adjacent 505 Dorchester Avenue building. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
505 Dorchester Avenue: Proposed as a 12-story, 198-foot tall (including mechanical 
penthouse and screens), 487,400 GFA sf mixed use laboratory, research & development, office, 
and retail building, including 156 bicycle parking spaces. The balance of the required bicycle 
parking (64 spaces) and all associated and propose vehicle parking for 505 Dorchester Avenue 
are included within the parking garage located at 65 Ellery Street and 75 Ellery Street. 
 
The Project is consistent with the criteria specified in Section 80C-4 of the Code for the 
approval of planned development areas in that the underlying zoning does not prohibit planned 
development areas, and the Project Site is not located in a residential zoning district. Further, 
this Development Plan generally conforms to the plan for this area, including without limitation, 
the BPDA PLAN: Dot Ave. and PLAN South Boston Dorchester Ave. Transportation Plan; and 
on balance, nothing in this Development Plan will be injurious to the neighborhood or otherwise 
detrimental to the public welfare. This Development Plan furthers the goals of the neighborhood 
to create a vibrant, mixed-use, transit-oriented development. 
 
Plans showing the architectural elements of the building(s) comprising the Project 
entitled “Appendix A1 65 Ellery Plans”, “Appendix A2 75 Ellery Plans”, and “Appendix A3 505

The Proponent is seeking approval by the Boston Planning & Development

General 
Description of 
Proposed 
Project 
The Proponent proposes to demolish the existing buildings on the Project 
Site, relocate and/or improve an existing Eversource/MBTA electrical 
substation structure and an MBTA spur track, and construct on the Project 
Site a mixed-use project with uses that are designed to include life sciences 
uses, research and development uses, office uses, retail/restaurant/commercial 
uses, and open space uses. The Project is comprised of two buildings 
collectively containing approximately 812,000 square feet in the aggregate, 
including approximately 10,000 square feet of space that is designed for uses 
including retail/restaurant/commercial uses and the balance of which is 
designed for life sciences/office/research and development space. The Project 
includes a subsurface parking structure containing up to 487 parking spaces. 
The Project will create privately-owned open spaces that will collectively 
comprise approximately 41,000 square feet (approximately 23% of the 
Project Site). The open spaces include a shared-use path, which 
accommodates pedestrians, bicycles, and wheelchairs, spanning from 
Cambridge Street to D Street (the “Shared-Use Path”). 
Public Benefits 
The Project will feature public benefits including (i) creation of a transit-
oriented development on an existing, auto-centric site that has been closed 
off for decades, (ii) creation of privately-owned open space open to the 
public on approximately 23% of the Project Site (approximately 41,000 
square feet), including a Shared-Use Path that will enhance access to/from 
the MBTA’s Sullivan Square Station, the emerging neighborhood west of 
Rutherford Avenue, and the surrounding community, (iii) reduction of on-
site impervious area by approximately 28%, (iv) establishing a ground-floor

edges and Shared-Use Path, including seating and places for gathering, (v) 
creating a buffer against noise, air quality, and visual impacts of the elevated

better pedestrian and cycling experience, (vii) establishing a gateway 
presence at the Cambridge Street corner, accentuating the pedestrian and

of new parking provided on site and improving pedestrian and bike 
infrastructure and connections, (xi) enhancing MBTA and Massport 
infrastructure currently on-site through relocation or upgrades as it may be 
arranged with the agencies at the Proponent’s cost, (xii) generating 
substantially increased property taxes and new tax revenues, (xiii) 
constructing energy-efficient buildings that will be certifiable, at a minimum, 
for LEED Gold, and (xiv) creating a significant number of job opportunities, 
including up to approximately 1,000 construction jobs and, upon 
stabilization, up to approximately 2,000 permanent jobs.

with an overall floor area ratio of 5.0, and a minimum of 15% Permeable 
Area of Lot. The Project, as designed, will comply with the requirements of 
the MU-3 District, as affected by this Development Plan.

1.0 Introduction 
In accordance with Sections 3-1A and 80C-3 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Zoning Code”), 
this plan constitutes the Master Plan for Planned Development Area No. [*] (the 
“Master PDA”) for the development of the parcels located at 35-45 Morrissey Boulevard, 55 
Morrissey Boulevard, and 75 Morrissey Boulevard in the Dorchester Neighborhood Zoning 
District (“Site”). As more particularly described below, the Master PDA contemplates the 
demolition of the three existing buildings on the Site, and the phased construction and 
redevelopment of multiple buildings and public realm (the “Proposed Project” and “Project”, 
a/k/a “35-75 Morrissey”), which are currently expected to be built in phases over an 
approximately 5 to 10 year period. The Master PDA encompasses approximately 8.9 acres of 
area of land referred to herein as the “Master PDA Area.” A figure depicting the location of the 
Master PDA Area is included as Exhibit A. The legal description and survey plan of the Master 
PDA Area are included as Exhibit B. 
 
The Master PDA Area is comprised entirely of land owned by Morrissey CFL Holdings, LLC. 
 
The Master PDA Area, which is approximately one-tenth of a mile away from the JFK/UMass 
MBTA Station, is within the Columbia-Morrissey Community Commercial Subdistrict 
(“Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict”), which was recently established in order to allow the 
creation of PDAs. The Master PDA will open the possibility for a project that will introduce up 
to 1.56 million gross square feet1 of mixed-use development that will convert a largely 
underutilized area into a thriving research, residential, office, and retail location with new public 
open spaces and publicly accessible internal roads and bicycle paths that will connect the Master 
PDA Area to the surrounding areas. By enabling (1) the development of research & development 
and office space that will lead to the creation of new, high paying jobs and training opportunities 
for neighborhood students, and (2) the addition of housing units, including affordable units, and 
public space where none had existed, the Master PDA will further the goals for which the 
Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict was created, which include the provision of “public benefits to 
the Dorchester community, including the creation of new job opportunities” and the 
“encourage[ment] of economic development.” Zoning Code § 65-28, as recently amended. 
Likewise, although the objectives for PDAs in the Dorchester Neighborhood District are written 
in the disjunctive, the Proposed Project will help realize each and every one of them – i.e., “(a) 
diversification and expansion of Dorchester's economy and job opportunities through economic 
activity, such as private investment in manufacturing, commercial uses, or research and 
development; (b) creation of new job opportunities and establishment of educational facilities, 
career counseling, or technical assistance providing instruction or technical assistance in fields 
related to such jobs; or (c) improvements to the urban design characteristics and aesthetic 
character of the development PDA Area and its surroundings, and the enhancement of existing 
open space or the creation of new open space.” Zoning Code § 65-31.

2.0 Master PDA Area Description 
 
The northern tip of the Master PDA Area is approximately one-tenth of a mile to the south of the 
JFK/UMass MBTA Station. The Master PDA Area includes the following three properties (1) 
35-45 Morrissey Boulevard, which is improved with a one-story brick commercial building that 
is occupied by a Star Market grocery store and a liquor store; (2) 55 Morrissey Boulevard, which 
is improved with a two-story brick building that is entirely occupied by Beasley Media Group; 
and (3) 75 Morrissey Boulevard, which is improved with a one-story commercial office building 
that has been vacant for several years and a surface parking lot. The Master PDA Area 
encompasses approximately 8.9 acres. The Master PDA Area is bounded to the south by the 
former Boston Globe headquarters (now The BEAT), to the west by the Southeast Expressway 
(Interstate 93), to the north by two residential buildings, and to the east by Morrissey Boulevard. 
The Proposed Project currently contemplates the demolition of the three existing buildings on the 
Site and the construction of seven new buildings that will serve the following uses: life sciences 
(research and development, general office, product development, prototype laboratory, research 
laboratory, light manufacturing, and the accessory keeping of animals incidental to laboratory 
and research and development use), multi-family residential, retail, and community (e.g., a 
community park). 
The legal description and survey plan of the Master PDA Area are attached as Exhibit B. 
 
3.0 The Proposed Project 
 
The Proposed Project reimagines the Master PDA Area as a vibrant mixed-use neighborhood, 
thereby opening significant opportunities to infuse the Master PDA Area with a variety of 
offerings for both public and private uses. As illustrated in the conceptual site plan at Exhibit C, 
this Master PDA proposes seven (7) new buildings on the Site, four of which will house research 
and development/life science uses and three of which will consist of multi-family housing units, 
with the building ground floors providing a mix of restaurant, retail and/or public space. The 
Proposed Project contemplates the creation of a new roadway network and new bicycle and 
pedestrian pathways within the Master PDA Area; the development of other publicly available 
space, including four (4) street-level community recreation spaces (totaling approximately 1.27 
acres), with landscaping and seating for use by shoppers, area employees, and area residents; and

4.0 Planning Objectives and Character of Redevelopment 
 
 
The Master PDA is intended to allow a Proposed Project that will further the objectives of the 
newly created Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict, which include the provision of “public benefits 
to the Dorchester community, including the creation of new job opportunities” and the 
“encourage[ment] of economic development” (Zoning Code § 65-28, as recently amended), and 
the objectives for PDAs in the Dorchester Neighborhood District, which include “(a) 
diversification and expansion of Dorchester's economy and job opportunities through economic 
activity, such as private investment in manufacturing, commercial uses, or research and 
development; (b) creation of new job opportunities and establishment of educational facilities, 
career counseling, or technical assistance providing instruction or technical assistance in fields 
related to such jobs; or (c) improvements to the urban design characteristics and aesthetic 
character of the development site and its surroundings, and the enhancement of existing open 
space or the creation of new open space” (Zoning Code § 65-31)). 
 
The Proposed Project’s design aims to create a vibrant nucleus of innovative workspace, active 
community amenities, and public realm in the Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict. The Proposed 
Project will reinvigorate a stale stretch of Morrissey Boulevard with vibrant life sciences offices, 
residential, retail, exterior public open space, streetscaping, and improved circulation for all 
modes of movement and circulation in the neighborhood. And, the Proposed Project will pair 
well with newly developed 135 Morrissey Boulevard; draw people onto, into, and through the 
Master PDA Area, forging a better connection with the surrounding neighborhood; capitalize on 
the nearby JFK/UMass MBTA station; and add more cohesiveness to the Master PDA Area and 
surrounding context. 
 
4.1 Land Use 
 
 
The design reimagines the Master PDA Area, which is a decadent area in need of revitalization, 
into an accessible, welcoming, and inclusive mixed-use development that will promote economic 
development, high paying careers, and training opportunities. The Proposed Project is currently 
anticipated to include up to 1.56M GFA of new buildings in addition to a new roadway network 
and publicly accessible open spaces. Approximately 54% of the Master PDA Area is proposed as 
public realm/open space and publicly accessible roadway networks. 
 
The blend of lab, office, residential, retail, community and a variety of publicly accessible open 
space will establish a vibrant and active new neighborhood. The newly created infrastructure will 
integrate and connect to the surrounding neighborhood context, creating a destination for the 
larger community driven by new retail offerings and publicly accessible open spaces. Central to 
the retail will be a new grocery store, replacing the aging existing store and continuing to serve 
the surrounding community. 
 
 
 

 
10 
 
4.2 Urban Design 
 
Much of the Master PDA Area is currently private, set off from and disconnected with the 
surrounding community, and offers minimal opportunities for jobs or job training, no residential 
units, and no meaningful open space. The parcel at 35-45 Morrissey Boulevard is currently 
improved with an old and unattractive building occupied by a Star Market grocery store and a 
liquor store; these uses are intended to be relocated to a new building in Phase 2 of the Project 
and the existing building demolished; 55 Morrissey Boulevard is currently improved with a two-
story brick building that is entirely occupied by Beasley Media Group – this building will 
ultimately be demolished; and 75 Morrissey Boulevard has a one-story commercial office 
building, which has been vacant for several years, and a surface parking lot. Overall, the 
approximately 8.9-acre Master PDA Area is highly underutilized, and does not come close to 
providing the type of economic development, jobs, housing, retail, and publicly available spaces 
that it is capable of offering. The Proposed Project intends to change the status quo, and convert 
this largely dormant area into a welcoming and inclusive public realm, a vibrant new workplace 
hub for the life sciences industry, additional housing, and much needed community spaces for 
the neighborhood. 
 
The Master PDA Area will be defined by the newly created street network. Main Street will 
serve as the primary artery running north/south through the Project Site and parallel to Morrissey 
Blvd. Three (3) perpendicular streets will provide access points connecting back to Morrissey 
Blvd. and a service road along the western perimeter of the Site will interconnect all the new 
roadways creating an entirely new neighborhood grid. The newly created blocks will provide 
defined spaces for buildings as well as publicly accessible open space. Street widths will be 
ample and define an appropriate scale and separation between buildings, giving appropriate room 
for vehicular circulation as well as pedestrian pathways, bike lanes, loading zones, 
landscaping/trees, and furnishing/café zones within the street right of ways. All newly created 
streets will follow Boston Complete Streets Design Guidelines. Newly created view corridors 
will extend unobstructed from the JFK/UMass MBTA Station through the Master PDA Area and 
to The BEAT (former Boston Globe Building) at the south end of the Site. Building frontages 
will be located on Main Street, drawing attention away from Morrissey Blvd. and providing a 
more insulated and welcoming front door to the new buildings and open spaces. 
 
The varying building use types will provide opportunities to create architectural diversity in the 
character of the buildings. Retail uses on the ground floor will draw visitors into the storefronts 
and activate the streetscapes throughout the Site. Building massing will utilize selective setbacks 
above podium levels along Main Street, helping to further improve the primary view corridor 
and provide greater open sky visibility. Building heights will scale upwards towards the north 
end of the Site and approaching the MBTA station in an effort to locate the greatest density 
adjacent to the highly proximate public transportation and away from surrounding 
neighborhoods. The massings of the buildings also take into consideration the effects of shadow 
and sunlight on the thermal comfort of the exterior spaces, promoting heartily designed 
landscapes and public realm that offer opportunities for use year-round. 
 

 
11 
 
In addition to the roadways, four (4) new dedicated park spaces will be created to further define 
the urban landscape of Master PDA Area. Parks will be located throughout the development Site 
to ensure open space are delivered within each phase of construction. A compliment of 
hardscape and softscape elements will define the park spaces and provide opportunities for 
programing that will benefit the community. 
 
Parking entrances and loading will be primarily relegated to the side streets and rear service road, 
limiting the amount of commercial traffic on the pedestrian-focused Main Street. The new 
perpendicular streets will also align with proposed roadways as part of the Dorchester Bay City 
development on the east side of Morrissey Blvd. 
 
When complete, the development will form a key link from the Columbia/Savin Hill 
Neighborhood to UMass, Bay City, and waterfront areas. 
 
See Conceptual site plan and renderings at Exhibits C-D. 
 
4.3 Public Realm 
 
4.3.1 Open Space 
 
A primary design goal of the Proposed Project is to maximize publicly accessible open space that 
will serve the community and help define the character of the newly created neighborhood. In 
total, the Proposed Project will include approximately 1.27 acres of primary open space, spread 
across four (4) dedicated parks with landscaping and seating for use by shoppers, area 
employees, and area residents; Approximately 4.7 acres and 54% of the Master PDA Area 
includes publicly accessible open spaces, public realm, and roadways. Open space will not only 
provide landscaped areas to compliment the building structures, but also support a variety of 
community specific programing as further described in the following section. 
 
Parks will include a balance of hard and softscape with ample trees, planting areas and hardscape 
elements such as benches and pathways. Local art installations are envisioned to compliment the 
hard and soft scape and provide an opportunity for community artists to showcase their work. 
Water features will provide unique visual interest and a place to cool down on hot summer days, 
and multiple lawn areas are designed for lounging or hosting community events. Dedicated areas 
with play equipment for children as well as enclosed areas for pet recreation will provide a space 
for all members of the community to play, relax, and connect with one another. 
 
In addition to parks, newly created streets include ample landscape areas and trees along with 
bench seating and café zones, further bolstering the open space offerings throughout the Site. 
 
Open spaces have been thoughtfully positioned throughout the development to ensure each 
construction phase includes a primary open space such that members of the community can 
benefit from the newly created open space even as future phases of development are still under 
construction. 
 
See Conceptual Site Plan at Exhibit C and Conceptual Renderings at Exhibit D.

4.3.2 Programming 
 
Opportunities to support various types of programing are contemplated within the public spaces 
envisioned in the Proposed Project. 
 
The Community Park at the south side of the Proposed Project serves as the gateway from the 
adjacent Savin Hill neighborhood and a vital connection to the adjacent 135 Morrissey Blvd. 
(The BEAT) project. In this park, opportunities for large scale art installations and support for 
music or other cultural events are envisioned within the context of the larger park space, 
including landscaped areas and meandering pathways. 
 
The Civic Plaza highlights the primary entrance into the Proposed Project and draws visitors into 
the Project’s primary retail component, the grocery store. Active zones with unique art 
installations and water features are envisioned as places for gathering and engaging, while 
shaded seating areas provide an opportunity for rest and relaxation. Support for semi-permanent 
kiosk structures will allow rotating vendors to take advantage of the prominent location on the 
Site. Events such as farmer’s markets, outdoor fitness and recreation activities can also be 
supported by the open spaces in this park. 
 
The Family Park at the north end of the Site offers programming opportunities for families to 
allow children to play in a safe and inviting setting. Open lawn areas will allow for ample room 
to gather while a dog run will provide for contained pet friendly areas. 
 
Along Main Street, the activated café zones are insulated from vehicular and bike traffic 
allowing retailers to establish both an indoor and outdoor presence along an enlivened Main 
Street. 
 
As retail is a major component of a robust public realm, the Proposed Project will aim to support 
local small businesses and prioritize W/MBE shops to bring a rich and diverse mix of food and 
beverage offerings to the Master PDA Area, and to meet other retail needs.

4.4 Resiliency 
 
The Master PDA Area is within the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District (“CFROD”), the 
requirements for which are set forth in Article 25A of the Zoning Code. The Proposed Project 
will comply with the Minimum Sea Level Rise-Design Flood Elevation set forth in Article 25A 
and any other requirements and limitations set forth therein. Lowest occupiable floor elevations 
of all buildings within the Master PDA Area have been set to 21.5 feet BCB to meet the SLR-
DFE recommendations and to provide two-feet of freeboard above the SLE-BFE. For parts of 
buildings located below 21.5 feet, BCB appropriate flood protection measures will be employed 
to mitigate flooding risk. 
 
Further, additional site resilience measures including permeable pavement, bioretention, 
extensive landscape areas and subgrade infiltration systems are contemplated to further mitigate 
the effects of sea level rise and climate change.

4.5 Sustainability 
 
To promote sustainability, the Proposed Project shall be designed to comply with the 
requirements of Article 37 (Green Buildings) of the Zoning Code to achieve the following: 
• Satisfaction of a minimum of LEED Gold Certifiable standards for all buildings within 
the Proposed Project; 
• Electrification of all building systems for normal operation of commercial lab, office, and 
residential uses, including the following heating and cooling systems: 
o Air source heat pumps 
o Exhaust source heat pumps 
o Ground source heat pumps; 
• Completion of a District Energy Feasibility Study in accordance with the City of Boston 
Smart Utilities plan, which shall include consideration of: 
o Geoexchange (“geothermal”) applications 
o Peak load shaving strategy 
o District energy loop; 
• A high-performance building envelope to reduce energy consumption; 
• High indoor air quality (IAQ) and daylit interior spaces; 
• Additional density within an urban core to reduce suburban sprawl; 
• Maximization of open space and an accessible public realm, both outdoors and indoors; 
• Enhanced access to existing neighborhood pedestrian and bicycle networks; 
• Outdoor space for building occupants; 
• Walkable retail options for residents and neighborhood visitors; 
• Enhanced access to nearby public transit infrastructure to reduce the trip generation of 
cars to the Master PDA Area; 
• On-site stormwater retention and groundwater recharge in accordance with City of 
Boston requirements.

payments to the City’s Housing and Jobs Trusts, and is committed to working 

 
19 
 
with local elected officials and community stakeholders to direct the linkage 
payments to local, Columbia-Morrissey/Dorchester Neighborhood, housing and 
jobs needs; 
o The Proposed Project will generate new annual real estate tax revenues for the 
City of Boston with the delivery of each phase. 
• The Proposed Project is expected to create construction jobs during the building phase; 
permanent jobs relating to life sciences, restaurant, residential administration and retail; 
and the opportunity for a pipeline of locally sourced jobs and careers. 
• The Proposed Project will support the local and regional economy by providing 
additional life science and office space to meet the increasing demand in the Columbia-
Morrissey Subdistrict. 
The specific project benefits associated with each component of the Proposed Project shall be 
included in the 80B filing for such building or Project phase. 
 
6.0 Technical Studies Performed in Support of Development of the Master PDA 
 
6.1 Traffic 
A transportation study has been developed to understand impacts associated with the Project and 
to help devise a comprehensive transportation mitigation and improvement plan in the vicinity of 
the Project that supports future operations of the Project and provides area-wide transportation 
improvements to the Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict of Boston. A major emphasis of this 
proposed redevelopment effort focuses on area mobility, including improved access and 
circulation to support the Master PDA Area and abutting properties, access to key transit nodes 
(namely, the JFK/UMass MBTA Station), and the significant network of pedestrian and bicycle 
infrastructure improvements. These elements are at the forefront of the analysis and future 
planning. Within the Project boundary, all new streets have been designed to meet Boston 
Complete Streets guidance and promote safe pedestrian, bicycle, and vehicular circulation. As 
the site is located one-tenth of a mile from the JFK/UMass MBTA Station, an emphasis will be 
placed on encouraging the use of public transportation for employees, visitors, and residents. 
 
It is understood that significant infrastructure improvements are contemplated for Morrissey 
Blvd. which will significantly alter the existing infrastructure in an effort to improve traffic and 
mobility issues within the neighborhood as a result of current and future projects. The Proposed 
Project provides for ample flexibility in adapting to changing infrastructure components along 
Morrissey Blvd., and there will be continued collaboration with the appropriate local and state 
authorities to provide input and resources as appropriate to facilitate these future improvements. 
Further, the Project is committed to help fund future improvements to the infrastructure along 
Morrissey Blvd., Kosciuszko Circle and at the JFK/UMass MBTA Station to mitigate the direct 
impacts of the Project. 
 
A more detailed analysis is included in the Transportation Study that is included as Appendix A. 
 
 
 

 
20 
 
6.2 Shadow 
The following summarizes the shadow impacts of the Proposed Project presented in this Master 
PDA. A more detailed visual analysis is shown in the Shadow Study that is included as 
Appendix B. 
Careful consideration has been given to the massing and heights of the Proposed Project to 
provide thermal comfort in the public spaces on Site, as well as limit the effect of new shadows 
on the surrounding community. As the Site is bounded to the west by Interstate 93 and east by 
Morrissey Boulevard, the new shadows cast fall primarily on these thoroughfares and no new 
shadows from the Project are cast on to the surrounding residential neighborhoods. During the 
summer months, shadows cast on the new public open spaces on Site are minimal during mid-
day hours, but also provide for shaded periods in the late afternoon and early evening when 
temperatures are at their peak. In the spring and fall seasons the on site parks experience 
shadows for periods of the day, but at alternate times allowing for some parks to provided shaded 
enjoyment while others to provide enjoyment in full sunlight. 
7.0 Effect of Master PDA 
 
7.1 Zoning 
The Proposed Project is located in the Dorchester Neighborhood Zoning District, the Community 
Commercial District (“CC”) Subdistrict, the Greenbelt Protection Overlay District (“GPOD”), 
the Restricted Parking District (“RPD”), and the CFROD. As noted, the Master PDA Area is also 
included in the newly created Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict. As shown on the Survey, Exhibit 
B, the Master PDA Area contains more than 5 acres of land, making it eligible, pursuant to 
Article 3-1A.a of the Zoning Code, for Master PDA approval through this submission. 
 
This Master PDA sets forth the zoning regulations for all elements of the Project for the Master 
PDA Area. Upon approval by the Boston Planning and Development Agency and the Boston 
Zoning Commission, any 80B filing relating to a building or Project phase within the Master 
PDA Area that is consistent with this PDA will be presumed to be consistent with the Zoning 
Code. 
 
7.2 Parcels 
The Master PDA Area is an assemblage of various legal lots which are all owned in fee by the 
proponent. In order to implement the Project, it is contemplated that new legal lots will be 
created and one or more may be leased or conveyed to third parties. 
 
Notwithstanding that lots may be in separate legal ownership and separated by streets, the Height 
and FAR maximum set forth in this Master PDA shall apply to the Master PDA Area as a whole 
and not to each individual lot, and a Certification of Consistency may be issued for each separate 
building; provided that non-compliance by a particular building shall not affect compliance by 
any other currently existing building or a building for which a Certification of Consistency has 
been issued. 
 

 
21 
 
7.3 Development Review 
Each building component of the Proposed Project within the Master PDA Area will be required 
to undergo design review subsequent to the submission of one or more Project Notification 
Forms for the Project (“80B Review), as well as the submission of an individual PDA 
Development Plan relating to the same (“80C PDA Development Plan”). In addition, review of 
environmental impacts will be studied during the 80B Review process, taking into account any 
technical studies already performed. 
 
The Proposed Project will also be subject to review under Zoning Code Articles 28 (Boston 
Civic Design Commission review), 37 (Green Buildings), and 25A (resiliency review).

1.1 
Overview 
The Project site is located on three adjacent parcels addressed as 35-75 Morrissey Boulevard. 
The approximately 10 acres site is bounded by Interstate 93 to the west, the Beat mixed-use 
development to the south, the Hub25 residential buildings to the north, and William T. 
Morrissey Boulevard (Morrissey Boulevard) to the east. The MBTA Red Line JFK/UMass Station 
is located approximately 1,000 feet to the north.

that will include a grocery store, and approximately 585 units of residential housing. The Project 
will also include approximately 901 parking spaces in a below grade parking structure.

1.1.3 
Study Methodology 
The Existing Condition analysis includes an inventory of the existing transportation conditions, 
such as traffic characteristics, parking, curb usage, transit, pedestrian circulation, bicycle 
facilities, loading, and site conditions. Existing counts for vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians 
were collected at the study area intersections. A traffic data collection effort forms the basis for 
the transportation analysis conducted as part of this evaluation. 
The future transportation conditions analysis evaluates potential transportation impacts 
associated with the Project. The long-term transportation impacts are evaluated for the year 
2029, based on a seven-year horizon from the year of the filing of this traffic study. 
♦ The No-Build (2029) Condition analysis includes traffic growth associated with specific 
developments (not including the Project) and transportation improvements that are 
planned in the vicinity of the Project Site. 
♦ The Build (2029) Condition analysis includes a net increase in traffic volume due to the 
addition of Project-generated trip estimates to the traffic volumes developed as part of 
the No-Build (2029) Condition analysis. The transportation study identifies expected 
impacts to roadway, parking, transit, pedestrian, and bicycle accommodations, as well as 
loading and service accommodations. 
The final part of the transportation study identifies measures to mitigate Project-related impacts 
and to address any traffic, pedestrian, bicycle, transit, safety, or construction-related issues that 
are necessary to accommodate the Project. 
An evaluation of short-term traffic impacts associated with construction activities is also 
provided. 
1.2 
Existing Condition 
This section includes descriptions of existing study area roadway geometries, intersection traffic 
control, peak-hour vehicular and pedestrian volumes, average daily traffic volumes, transit 
availability, parking, curb usage, and loading conditions. 
1.2.1 
Existing Roadway Conditions 
The study area includes, but is not limited to, the following roadways, which are categorized 
according to the MassDOT Office of Transportation Planning functional classifications. 
Morrissey Boulevard is a two-way, six-lane roadway located east of the Project site. It is 
classified as an urban principal arterial roadway under the jurisdiction of the Department of 
Conservation and Recreation (DCR) and runs in a predominately north-south direction between 
Kosciuszko Circle to the north in South Boston and Gallivan Boulevard to the south in 
Dorchester. A raised median separates the northbound and southbound traffic along the main 
line. Within proximity of the Project site, Morrissey Boulevard has access roadways along the 
outside of the mainline. These access roadways allow for local access to businesses without 
impeding the throughput of the mainline. The Morrissey Boulevard southbound Access Road 
consists of two lanes just north of the Project Site and expands to three lanes, directly adjacent 
of the Project site. The Morrissey Boulevard northbound Access Road consists primarily of two

lanes. In the vicinity of the site, on-street parking is prohibited, and sidewalks are provided along 
the exterior edge of each Access Road segments. An elevated pedestrian bridge exists to the 
north of the Project site and provides a safe crossing point for pedestrians. 
Old Colony Avenue is a two-way, predominantly four-lane roadway located to the north of the 
Project site. In the vicinity of the project site, Old Colony Avenue is a two-way, two-lane 
roadway with no raised median. It is classified as a principal arterial roadway under the City of 
Boston’s jurisdiction and runs predominately in a north-south direction between Dorchester 
Avenue to the north in South Boston and its intersection with Mount Vernon Street to the south 
in Dorchester. In the vicinity of the site, on-street parking is prohibited, and sidewalks are 
provided along both sides of the roadway. 
Mount Vernon Street is a two-way, two-lane roadway located to the north-east of the Project 
site. Mount Vernon Street is classified as a major collector roadway under DCR jurisdiction and 
runs predominately in an east-west direction between its intersection with Old Colony Avenue 
to the east and its intersection with University Drive to the west. In the vicinity of the site, on-
street parking is prohibited, and sidewalks are provided along both sides of the roadway. A 
raised median separates the eastbound and westbound traffic. 
Bianculli Boulevard is a two-way, four-lane roadway located to the southeast of the Project Site. 
It is classified as a local roadway and owned by the University of Massachusetts (UMass). The 
roadway runs in a predominately east-west direction between University Drive to the east and 
Morrissey Boulevard to the west. On-street parking is prohibited along the entire length of the 
roadway and a sidewalk is provided along the north side of the roadway. The Harborwalk 
shared-use path is provided along the south side of the roadway for pedestrian and bicycle use. 
1.2.2 
Existing Intersection Conditions 
The existing study area intersections are described below. Intersection characteristics such as 
traffic control, lane usage, and pedestrian facilities, are described. 
Bianculli Boulevard/Morrissey Boulevard is a signalized, four-legged intersection with four 
approaches. The Bianculli Boulevard westbound approach consists of three lanes, two exclusive 
left-turn lanes, and one channelized right-turn lane under signalized control with approximately 
50 feet of storage. The Morrissey Boulevard northbound approach consists of four lanes, three 
exclusive through lanes, and one channelized right-turn lane under signalized control. The 
Morrissey Boulevard southbound approach consists of three exclusive through lanes. The 
Morrissey Boulevard Access Road south-eastbound approach consists of four lanes, two 
exclusive left-turn lanes, one shared through/bare right-turn lane, and one exclusive right-turn 
lane. A dedicated U-turn lane is provided approximately 550 feet north of the intersection, 
allowing northbound vehicles to reverse course. This movement is under stop control. 
Crosswalks are provided across the south and east side of the intersection. All crosswalks have 
pedestrian signal equipment, curb ramps, and tactile warning panels.

1.4.5 
Trip Generation Methodology 
Determining the future trip generation of the Project is a complex, multi-step process that 
produces an estimate of vehicle trips, transit trips, and walk/bicycle trips associated with a 
proposed development and a specific land use program. A project’s location and proximity to 
different travel modes determines how people will travel to and from a site. 
To estimate the number of trips expected to be generated by the Project, data published by the 
Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE) in the Trip Generation Manual1 were used. ITE 
provides data to estimate the total number of unadjusted vehicular trips associated with the 
Project. In an urban setting well-served by transit, adjustments are necessary to account for 
other travel modes such as walking, bicycling, and transit. 
To estimate the unadjusted number of vehicular trips for the Project, the following ITE land use 
codes (LUC) were used: 
Land Use Code 221 – Multifamily Housing Mid Rise. High-rise multifamily housing includes 
apartments, townhouses, or condominiums that have between three and ten levels. They are 
likely to have one or more elevators. Calculations of the number of trips uses ITE’s average rate 
per unit. 
Land Use Code 222 – Multifamily Housing High Rise. High-rise multifamily housing includes 
apartments, townhouses, or condominiums that have more than 10 levels. They are likely to 
have one or more elevators. Calculations of the number of trips uses ITE’s average rate per unit. 
Land Use Code 760 – Research & Development Center. Research and development centers are 
facilities or groups of facilities devoted to research and development activities. The range of 
specific types of businesses contained in this land use varies significantly. Research and 
development centers may contain offices and light fabrication areas. Calculations of the number 
of trips use ITE’s average rate per 1,000 sf. 
Land Use Code 820 – Shopping Center. The Shopping Center land use code is defined as an 
integrated group of commercial establishments that is planned, developed, owned, and 
managed as a unit. Shopping center trip generation estimates are based on average vehicle 
rates per square footage of retail space. Calculations of the number of trips use ITE’s average 
rate per 1,000 sf. 
1.4.5.1 
Internal Capture Trips 
A key characteristic of large multi-use developments such as the Project is that trips among the 
various land uses can be made on site and these internal trips are not made on the surrounding 
roadway network. For example, somebody living within a development may work or choose to 
shop within that development, reducing the potential for trips to be made throughout the

1.4.7 
Existing Trip Generation 
When assessing a site with existing, active land uses, it is standard practice to estimate existing 
trips and subtract those trips from the projected new future trips. The result of this process 
yields “net new” trips that become the basis for traffic analysis. For example, the vacating of an 
industrial building that is replaced by a mixed use development. The existing uses on this site, 
except for the supermarket, are either vacant or generating very little trips. 
The existing supermarket, currently at 45 Morrissey Boulevard, is actively generating trips 
throughout the day. The Project includes a new supermarket within Building C to replace the 
existing services. In this instance, the trip generation associated with these retail uses are 
expected to be the same in the future as the trip generation was during the data collection. 
Therefore, these uses are not included in the Project trip generation. The shopping center trip 
generation includes the new retail space within the Project that is beyond the existing 
supermarket.

1.5 
Vehicle Operations Analysis 
The criterion for evaluating vehicle operations is level of service (LOS), which is determined by 
assessing average delay experienced by vehicles at intersections and along intersection 
approaches. Trafficware’s Synchro (version 11) software package was used to calculate average 
delay and associated LOS at the study area intersections. This software is based on the vehicle 
operational analysis methodology of the Transportation Research Board’s (TRB’s) 2000 Highway 
Capacity Manual (HCM). One of the study intersections is a roundabout; therefore, that location 
was analyzed using the SIDRA software package instead of Synchro. Field observations were 
performed to collect intersection geometry such as number of turning lanes, lane length, and 
lane width that were then incorporated into the operations analysis. 
LOS designations are based on average delay per vehicle for all vehicles entering an intersection. 
Table 1-7 displays the intersection LOS criteria. LOS A indicates the most favorable condition, 
with minimum traffic delay, while LOS F represents the worst condition, with significant traffic 
delay. LOS D or better is typically considered desirable during the peak hours of traffic in urban 
and suburban settings. However, LOS E or F is often typical for a stop-controlled minor street 
that intersects a major roadway and does not necessarily indicate that the operations at the 
intersection are poor or failing.

In addition to delay and LOS, the operational capacity and vehicular queues are calculated and 
used to further quantify traffic operations at intersections. The following describes these other 
calculated measures. 
The volume-to-capacity ratio (v/c ratio) is a measure of congestion at an intersection approach. 
A v/c ratio below one indicates that the intersection approach has adequate capacity to process 
the arriving traffic volumes over the course of an hour. A v/c ratio of one or greater indicates 
that the traffic volume on the intersection approach exceeds capacity. 
The 50th percentile queue length, measured in feet, represents the maximum queue length 
during a cycle of the traffic signal with typical (or median) entering traffic volumes. 
The 95th percentile queue, measured in feet, represents the farthest extent of the vehicle queue 
(to the last stopped vehicle) upstream from the stop line. This maximum queue occurs five 
percent, or less, of the time during the peak hour, and typically does not develop during off-

1.6 
Transit Capacity Analysis 
As presented in Section 1.2.8, transit service in the area includes the MBTA Red Line, Route 8, 
Route 16, and Route 41 buses, and the Project-generated transit trips are expected to use these 
MBTA services. The associated transit capacity evaluation presented below is focused on those 
routes. 
1.6.1 
Transit Analysis Methodology 
The V/C is the primary measurement to determine the impact to transit service from the 
Project. The V/C ratio is a measurement of the number of passengers divided by the planning 
capacity. A V/C ratio of 1.0 or higher means the transit service is at capacity and any additional 
passengers either cannot fit or will cause delays to service as passengers try to crowd onto the 
train or bus. To calculate the V/C, ridership and capacity were determined for the Existing 
Condition to evaluate how the transit service operates today. Then, like the process of 
projecting vehicular traffic, the future ridership and capacity was developed both for the No-
Build (2029) Condition, without the Project, and the Build (2029) Condition, with the Project. 
The MBTA defines their capacity standard as the planning capacity, which is the number of 
passengers that can comfortably fit on a train or bus. As defined in the MBTA’s Service and 
Delivery Policy, the planning capacity for a bus is calculated as 125 percent of the seated 
capacity during off-peak hours and 140 percent of the seated capacity during peak hours. Bus 
capacity was also compared to the MBTA bus profile sheets created under the Better Bus 
Project. A standard 40-foot bus, with 39 seats, has a planning capacity of 48 passengers per bus 
during off-peak hours and 55 passengers per bus during peak hours. A typical Red Line train car 
with 62 seats has a planning capacity of 92 passengers during off-peak hours and 161 
passengers during peak hours. 
1.6.2 
Transit Analysis Results 
Figure 1-18 through Figure 1-29 show the ridership by transit-vehicle trip throughout the day for 
bus Routes 8, 16 and 41, as well as the Red Line before and after JFK/UMass Station. The charts 
reflect ridership estimates under the Existing Condition, No-Build (2029) Condition, and Build 
(2029) Condition. 
The associated ridership and V/C ratios are provided in table format as an attachment to this 
document. It should be noted that the table data reflects average conditions over the half hour 
time periods, while individual buses may have higher loads and exceed capacity. The ridership 
and capacity were identified for activity before and after the nearby bus stops for each route. 
The V/C ratio is the primary measurement to determine the impact that the Project has on 
transit. The V/C ratio is a measurement of the number of passengers divided by the planning 
capacity. A V/C ratio of 1.0 or higher means the transit line is at capacity and any additional 
passengers either cannot fit or will cause delays to service as passengers try to crowd onto the 
bus. 
According to MBTA data and the methodology outlined in this report, the MBTA Red Line and

the Project, and passengers related to the Project within the existing capacity that is provided

Transportation Demand Management 
The Proponent is committed to implementing a robust TDM program to minimize automobile 
usage and Project related traffic impacts. The Proponent is prepared to take advantage of good 
transit access in marketing the Project Site to future tenants by working with them to 
implements TDM measures to encourage the use of non-vehicular modes of travel. 
BTD released a TDM Point System Tool in September 2021, for all large, new projects, that aims 
to reduce vehicle trips. In accordance with this new point system, the Proponent will choose 
TDM strategies that collectively meet the point level target for the Project Site. 
1.7.1 
Baseline TDM Strategies 
As required, the Proponent is committed to implementing all of the Baseline TDM strategies: 
♦ Joining the local Transportation Management Association (TMA) on behalf of commercial 
tenants; 
♦ Designating a member of the Project staff to serve as transportation coordinator (whose 
responsibilities may include other Project-related duties) to oversee the transportation 
issues, including parking, service and loading, and deliveries; 
♦ Providing orientation packets to new tenants containing information on available 
transportation, including transit routes and schedules, nearby vehicle sharing and bicycle 
sharing locations, and walking opportunities; 
♦ Providing an annual newsletter or bulletin promoting multimodal travel options and 
benefits; 
♦ Hosting at least two on-site annual events promoting multimodal travel; 
♦ Installing real-time transit information in building lobbies per BTD review; 
♦ Providing ride services, such as reimbursement of taxi or rideshare trips, outside of peak 
travel periods for tenants/employees who use sustainable transportation options; 
♦ Facilitate participation of tenants in the MBTA Perq Program 
♦ Providing tenants the option to lease or purchase building space without the inclusion of 
a market rate price for on-site parking; 
♦ Comply with the BTD Bike Parking Guidelines which includes short and long term bicycle 
parking, showers and changing facilities, and a monetary contribution to the Boston bike 
share system and space for a bike share station on site. 
1.7.2 
Impact TDM Strategies

TDM strategies: 
♦ Transit: Property owner or employer provides a subsidy for monthly MBTA transit 
passes;

Transportation Mitigation Measures 
The Proponent will continue to work with the City of Boston to create a Project that efficiently 
serves vehicle trips, improves the pedestrian environment, and encourages transit and bicycle 
use. The Proponent will construct new sidewalks adjacent to the Project Site in accordance with 
Boston Complete Streets Guidelines and requirements of the Americans with Disabilities Act and 
Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (ADA/AAB) to the extent feasible. This will include the 
reconstruction and widening of the sidewalks where possible, the installation of new, accessible 
ramps, improvements to street lighting where necessary, planting of street trees, and providing 
bicycle storage racks, where appropriate. 
The Proponent is responsible for preparation of the Transportation Access Plan Agreement 
(TAPA), a legal agreement between the Proponent and the BTD. The TAPA formalizes the 
findings of the transportation study, mitigation commitments, elements of access and physical 
design, TDM measures, and any other responsibilities that are agreed to by both the Proponent

and the BTD. Because the TAPA must incorporate the results of the technical analysis, it must be 
executed after these other processes have been completed. The proposed measures listed 
above and any additional transportation improvements to be undertaken as part of this Project 
will be defined and documented in the TAPA. 
1.9 
Evaluation of Short-term Construction Impacts 
The Proponent will also produce a Construction Management Plan (CMP) for review and 
approval by BTD. The CMP will detail the schedule, staging, parking, delivery, and other 
associated impacts of the construction of the Project. 
Most construction activities will be accommodated within the current Project Site boundaries. 
Details of the overall construction schedule, working hours, number of construction workers, 
worker transportation and parking, number of construction vehicles, and routes will be 
addressed in detail in the CMP to be filed with BTD in accordance with the City’s transportation 
maintenance plan requirements. 
To minimize transportation impacts during the construction period, the following measures will 
be considered for the CMP: 
♦ Limited construction worker parking on-site; 
♦ Encouragement of worker carpooling; 
♦ Consideration of a subsidy for MBTA passes for full-time employees; and 
♦ Providing secure spaces on-site for workers’ supplies and tools so they do not have to be 
brought to the site each day. 
The CMP to be executed with the City prior to commencement of construction will document all 
committed measures.

The Proponent is requesting approval of the Boston Redevelopment

III. Location of 
Proposed 
Project 
The PDA (the “Master Plan Area”) is comprised of discrete City of 
Boston Assessing Parcels No. 0203963050 (the “Northern Site”) and No. 
0203964000 (the “Southern Site”) located generally at the southwestern 
corner of the Austin Street/New Rutherford Avenue intersection in 
Boston’s Charlestown. A middle access driveway bisects the Master Plan 
Area and connects New Rutherford Avenue to a rear service driveway. 
The Building B site is a portion of the Northern Site. The Master Plan 
Area, including the Building B site, currently contains surface parking, 
which will be razed to facilitate development. 
IV. Proposed 
Project 
The Building B redevelopment program contemplates a new, up to 7-story 
building containing approximately 125 dwelling units and residential 
amenities, together with bicycle storage in accordance with City of 
Boston Bike Parking Guidelines, an urban plaza and lawn, a new 
connection across the Northern Site between New Rutherford Avenue and 
the rear service driveway, and related site and public realm improvements.
V. 
Public Benefits 
The Austin Street Lots Redevelopment Master Plan, including the 
Building B redevelopment program, contemplates a wide variety of public 
and community benefits, subject to design finalization and approval from 
appropriate governmental authorities. These benefits include revitalization 
of an underutilized site proximate to public transit (i.e., MBTA’s Orange 
Line Community College subway station and bus routes 92 and 93); an 
increase in Charlestown’s housing supply, including income-restricted 
dwelling units; significant open space providing recreational amenities for 
the Charlestown community; enhanced public realm elements with 
improved pedestrian and bicycle connectivity; sustainability features such 
as energy-efficient building systems, improved site permeability and 
stormwater treatment, reduced urban heat island impacts, and flood 
resiliency measures; and additional property tax revenue for the City of 
Boston.

governed by Article 25A. The Master Plan Area encompassing the 
Building B site contains more than 5 acres of land area and is PDA-
eligible due to its inclusion within Area PDA I. Approval of this PDA 
Development Plan would provide the zoning relief required for Building 
B within the Austin Street Lots Redevelopment Master Plan.
