FACT SHEET 
GILLETTE FORT POINT REDEVELOPMENT 
MASTER PLAN FOR PLANNED DEVELOPMENT AREA NO. X 
 
APPLICANT 
The Gillette Company, LLC, a Delaware limited liability company and 
a wholly-owned subsidiary of The Procter & Gamble Company, an Ohio 
corporation. 
 
PDA OVERLAY 
AREA 
An approximately 31.38-acre site, including the area below the mean high 
tide line as well as the 30.89-acre Project Site, generally bounded by the 
development known as 232 A Street to the north, A Street to the east, West 
Second Street and West Broadway to the south, and Foundry Street, 
Dorchester Avenue and the Fort Point Channel to the west. The Project Site 
presently is divided into three parcels by Dorchester Avenue and Foundry 
Street. 
 
PROJECT 
The Proposed Project contemplates the phased construction of up to 
20 new buildings consisting of approximately 5.74 million gross square 
feet of office, research and development, warehouse, manufacturing, 
residential, hotel, commercial (e.g. retail, restaurant or fitness center), 
electric power generation, community, cultural and other uses, open space, 
much of will be accessible to the public, and up to 4,489 accessory parking 
spaces, largely located in below-ground structured parking and a small 
number of parking spaces on certain streets within the Project Site (the 
“Proposed Project”). The Proposed Project will also feature significant 
public realm improvements including seven new dedicated open spaces, 
comprising a total of approximately 8.0 acres, and a new street network 
with on-street parking. 
 
DEVELOPMENT 
CONCEPT 
The Proposed Project will unlock a site that has been inaccessible to the 
public for more than 60 years, and connect it to surrounding 
neighborhoods, open spaces, the waterfront and public transportation. It 
will transform the existing industrial-oriented uses into a vibrant mixed-
use community that includes both residential and commercial uses, with 
active ground floors and welcoming view corridors. The Proposed Project 
will create a precedent-setting, climate-resilient development that 
supports the City’s environmental goals, include green infrastructure to 
address district stormwater concerns and promote coastal resilience by 
protecting much of the Project Site and the neighborhood beyond. It will 
develop a transit-oriented, sustainable neighborhood that improves 
circulation in the area, and contributes to a city that is welcoming, 
accessible, and inclusive. 

2 
 
 
 
PROPOSED USES Office, research and development, warehouse, light industrial, 
 manufacturing, residential, hotel, commercial (e.g., retail, entertainment, 
restaurant service, community, civic, educational, medical and institutional 
uses), electric power generation, community, cultural and other uses, as 
well as parking facilities and open space as further described in the Master 
Plan for the Planned Development Area No. X. 
PUBLIC 
BENEFITS 
Approximately 8.0 acres of new open space, including certain areas 
dedicated in perpetuity to the public. The Proposed Project will deliver 
passive and active open space, sustainable design and resilient building 
strategies, active and pedestrian-friendly uses, district-scale flood 
protection measures to protect from the adverse effects of sea level rise 
and storm surge, and site remediation. A new street network comprising 
public and private streets will provide access and connectivity through 
the Project Site for pedestrians, bicycles and vehicles. New affordable 
housing units will be delivered in compliance with the City’s 
Inclusionary Development Policy. Numerous new permanent jobs and 
temporary construction jobs will be created. The Proposed Project will 
also deliver significant Housing Exactions, Jobs Contributions 
Exactions, other Proposed Project-related mitigation benefits, and 
meaningful new tax revenues for the City of Boston.

SOLICITANTE 
The Gillette Company, LLC, una empresa de responsabilidad limitada 
de Delaware y filial controlada enteramente por The Procter & Gamble 
Company, una sociedad anónima de Ohio. 
 
ÁREA DE USO ESPECIAL DEL PDA 
 
Un terreno de aproximadamente 31.38 acres, incluida la zona por debajo de 
la línea de pleamar media, así como el emplazamiento del proyecto de 
30.89 acres, delimitado en general por el desarrollo conocido como 232 A 
Street al norte, A Street al este, West Second Street y West Broadway al 
sur, y Foundry Street, Dorchester Avenue y el canal de Fort Point al oeste. 
Actualmente, el emplazamiento del proyecto está dividido en tres lotes 
situados junto a Dorchester Avenue y Foundry Street. 
 
PROYECTO 
El proyecto propuesto contempla la construcción por etapas de hasta 20 
edificios nuevos de aproximadamente 5.74 millones de pies cuadrados 
edificados 
destinados 
a 
oficinas, 
investigación 
y 
desarrollo, 
depósitos, fabricación, viviendas, hoteles, comercios (p. ej., tiendas, 
restaurantes o gimnasios), generación de energía eléctrica, usos 
comunitarios, culturales y de otro tipo, espacios abiertos, gran parte de los 
cuales serán accesibles al público, y hasta 4,489 plazas de estacionamiento 
complementario, ubicadas en su mayor parte en espacios estructurados de 
estacionamiento subterráneo y un número pequeño de plazas de 
estacionamiento en algunas calles dentro del emplazamiento del proyecto 
(el «Proyecto propuesto»). El proyecto propuesto también incluirá mejoras 
significativas del espacio público, como siete nuevos espacios abiertos 
exclusivos, con una superficie total de aproximadamente 8.0 acres, y una 
nueva red de calles con estacionamiento en la vía pública. 
 
DESARROLLO 
CONCEPTO 
El proyecto propuesto liberará un predio que ha estado inaccesible al 
público durante más de 60 años y lo conectará con los barrios 
circundantes, los espacios abiertos, el paseo marítimo y el transporte 
público. Transformará los actuales usos orientados a la industria en una 
vibrante comunidad de usos mixtos que incluirá usos residenciales y 
comerciales, con plantas bajas activas y corredores con vistas atractivas. 
El proyecto propuesto sentará un precedente de desarrollo resiliente al 
clima que promueve las metas medioambientales de la ciudad, incluirá 
infraestructuras verdes para abordar los problemas de aguas pluviales del 
distrito y promoverá la resiliencia costera mediante la protección de gran 
parte del emplazamiento del proyecto y del resto del barrio. Desarrollará

circulación en la zona y hará su contribución a una ciudad hospitalaria,

espacios abiertos, tal como se describe con más detalle en el Plan Maestro

BENEFICIOS 
PÚBLICOS 
Aproximadamente 8.0 acres de nuevo espacio abierto, incluidas ciertas 
áreas destinadas al público a perpetuidad. El proyecto propuesto 
ofrecerá espacios abiertos pasivos y activos, un diseño sostenible y 
estrategias de construcción resilientes, usos activos y adaptados a los 
peatones, medidas de protección contra inundaciones para todo el 
distrito a fin de proteger la zona de los efectos adversos del aumento del 
nivel del mar y las marejadas, así como la rehabilitación del 
emplazamiento. Una nueva red de calles públicas y privadas brindará

peatones, las bicicletas y los vehículos. El proyecto incluirá nuevas 
viviendas asequibles de conformidad con la política de desarrollo

Dated: July 14, 2022 
 
1.0 
Introduction 
In December 2017, the President and Fellows of Harvard College, acting as Harvard University (together 
with its affiliates, “Harvard”), filed a Master Plan for Planned Development Area No. 115 (the “Original 
Master Plan”) with the Boston Redevelopment Authority d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency 
(the “BPDA”), which was approved by the BPDA and adopted by the City of Boston in March 2018. 
Subsequent to such approval and adoption of the Original Master Plan, Harvard Allston Land Company 
has selected Tishman Speyer ERC Developer, L.L.C. (the “Proponent”) to develop the Proposed Project 
(as defined below). 
 
In accordance with Sections 3-1A and 80C-3 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Zoning Code”), this plan 
constitutes an Amended and Restated Master Plan for Planned Development Area No. 115 (this “PDA 
Master Plan”) for the development of a portion of the Enterprise Research Campus on Western Avenue in 
the Allston neighborhood of Boston, and amends, restates and supersedes the Original Master Plan in its 
entirety. This PDA Master Plan covers an approximately 14.2-acre (approximately 619,402-square-foot) 
parcel of land referred to as the “PDA Area.” A figure depicting the location of the PDA Area in the context 
of the surrounding neighborhood is included as Exhibit A. The survey and legal description of the PDA 
Area are included as Exhibits B and C. All of the land comprised by the PDA Area is owned in fee by 
Harvard. 
 
As more particularly described below, this PDA Master Plan contemplates the construction of multiple 
buildings and other improvements (the “Proposed Project”), which may be built simultaneously or in 
phases. The Proposed Project consists of (i) the development of an approximately 9.4-acre portion of the 
PDA Area (consisting of approximately 6 acres to be developed as buildings, open space, and related 
improvements, and approximately 3.4 acres of streets and other enabling infrastructure) as shown on 
Exhibit D as the “Phase A PDA Area” pursuant to and in accordance with that certain “Phase A 
Development Plan for Planned Development Area No. 115” (the “Phase A Development Plan”) that is 
being submitted to the BPDA for approval concurrently with the submission of this PDA Master Plan (such 
redevelopment, the “Phase A Project”), and (ii) a second development phase within the PDA Area, 
consisting of the development of an approximately 4.8-acre portion of the PDA Area as shown on Exhibit 
D as the “Phase B PDA Area.” The second development phase (the “Phase B Project”) is subject to future 
Large Project Review under Article 80B of the Zoning Code and will require the submission and approval 
of a separate Planned Development Area Development Plan (the “Phase B Development Plan”). 
 

 
 
2 
The Original Master Plan provided for the development of the Phase A PDA Area and the use of the Phase 
B PDA Area for surface parking lots. The Original Master Plan is being amended and restated in this PDA 
Master Plan to incorporate certain changes in the proposed development within the Phase A PDA Area and 
to enable the Proponent to pursue the future redevelopment of the Phase B PDA Area. 
 
Review under Article 80B (Large Project Review) of the Zoning Code has been undertaken and completed 
with respect to the Phase A Project, subject to on-going review in accordance with BPDA Development 
Review Procedures. A Project Notification Form for development of the Phase A Project was filed with the 
BPDA on February 2, 2021. The BPDA issued a Scoping Determination for the Phase A Project under 
Section 80B of the Zoning Code on May 14, 2021. A Draft Project Impact Report for the Phase A Project 
was subsequently filed with the BPDA on July 28, 2021. On September 9, 2021 the Proponent filed drafts 
of this PDA Master Plan and the Phase A Development Plan. On November 23, 2021, the Proponent filed 
a Supplemental Information Document responding to comments on the Draft Project Impact Report. 
Review under Article 80B (Large Project Review) of the Zoning Code for the Phase B Project will be 
undertaken in the future. 
 
This PDA Master Plan: 
(i) sets forth a statement of the development concept for the PDA Area, including the planning objectives 
and character of the development, the proposed uses of the area, the range of dimensional requirements for 
each of the proposed structures, and the proposed phasing of construction, and 
(ii) provides for one or more PDA Development Plans to be submitted providing more specific information 
about the elements of the Proposed Project and components thereof. 
This PDA Master Plan consists of 22 pages of text plus attachments designated as Exhibits A through K. 
All references to this PDA Master Plan contained herein will pertain only to such pages and Exhibits. This 
PDA Master Plan shall be governed by the Zoning Code in effect as of the date hereof and, unless otherwise 
set forth herein, all references to terms defined by the Zoning Code will have the meanings set forth in 
Section 2A of the Zoning Code, as amended to the effective date hereof, and not as amended hereafter.

It is anticipated that construction of the Proposed Project will be phased as the Phase A Project and the

5.0 
Planning Objectives and Character of Development 
The following planning principles present a summary of the principles guiding the development of this 
PDA Master Plan. 
 5.1 Land Use 
The PDA Area and adjacent portions of the Harvard Enterprise Research Campus site are currently vacant, 
with some areas used from time to time as construction laydown and staging areas. Proposed future uses 
defined by the development of the PDA Area will result in the construction of a diverse mix of uses, 
including office, lab, research space, residential, retail, restaurant and other uses, as well as a range of 
publicly accessible open spaces. A complete list of allowed uses is included on Exhibit E and is described 
further in Section 4.2 above. 
The planning for the PDA Area focuses on goals that include establishing relationships between the future 
commercial and research tenants of the PDA Area and the teaching and research mission of Harvard. 
Simultaneously, the success of the PDA Area as an urban district will also be contingent on the 
establishment of a robust mixed-use development program including office, lab, research space, residential, 
retail, restaurant and other uses, as well as a range of publicly accessible open spaces. This type of mix is 
intended to ensure that the area is vibrant, with activity extending through the day and evening. 

 
 
9 
Along primary streets within the PDA Area, a high degree of porosity and public interface is desired. 
 5.2 Urban Design 
Architectural expression of buildings within the PDA Master Plan will be driven in large part by their 
individual and unique context within the overall PDA Master Plan, and the design of the future buildings 
should emphasize a variety of scale, style, and material to reflect such diversity of experience throughout 
the PDA Area. To this end, individual buildings are encouraged to find creative expression while complying 
with the dimensional requirements and urban design parameters set forth below and on Exhibit G. 
Buildings should create well-defined public spaces and maintain a human scale at the ground level. 
Distinctive, place specific design, durability, and long-term sustainability should drive the architectural 
character of all new construction. Architecture that is expressive of the new trends in housing and 
commercial uses, and derived from the unique mixed-use nature of this district, is encouraged. Façade 
materials and expressions must have appropriate detail and scale-giving elements to contribute to a 
distinctive urban context. A set of design guidelines, attached hereto as Exhibit H, manage how the 
buildings relate to each other and to the adjacent public realm. 
The blocks within the PDA Area are organized by streets, paths, and open spaces that are currently designed 
to break down existing impenetrable areas into a system of development blocks that guide future 
incremental growth. The blocks identify sites within which one or more buildings can be developed in the 
future. Each site can accommodate a variety of building footprints, perimeter open space and courtyards. 
The block plan allows for a mix of building types and scales to coexist in the PDA Area. As planning and 
tenancy evolve, the block plan may need to be adjusted, in accordance with Section 4.1 above. 
The Proposed Project will provide a range of public and community benefits, including new usable, publicly 
accessible open space, economic activity, improved circulation, and a mix of uses and housing options. The 
Proposed Project seeks to provide welcoming, programmable and inclusive open spaces that will 
themselves serve as social hubs and incubators. Additional public and community benefits as they relate to 
urban design are addressed in the Design Guidelines included on Exhibit H. 
Development within the PDA Area should clearly establish gateway treatments at key intersections, 
particularly those that intersect with Western Avenue such as at Cattle Drive. This may involve setback 
conditions or other physical or programmatic treatments that signal entrance to an important urban district 
apart from (although related to) the Harvard academic campus directly to the north. 
Access to internalized building services will be integrated into the landscape design, paving design, and 
architecture, thereby minimizing adverse impact on the pedestrian realm. The intersection between Cattle 
Drive, Science Drive, and the Project Greenway is envisioned as a key urban moment that will have a 
pedestrian focus and create the sense of a plaza or town square rather than a conventional street crossing. 
The arrangement of the buildings, streets, and Project Greenway will allow for the establishment of a critical 
mass and activate the space to create a lively environment in the early phases of development. 
Along the ground floor, the building edges facing Cattle Drive, Western Avenue, and East Drive are 
programmed to be active, both along the streets and along the Greenway. Interruptions to these open spaces 
and sidewalks are minimized through the consolidation of services and loading between buildings. To 
further enhance the character and usability of the publicly accessible open spaces, buildings are sited to 
account for wind conditions, daylight access, and sources of sound pollution. 

 
 
10 
In order to enhance the porosity of the PDA Area, pedestrian, bicycle, vehicular, and service access will be 
carefully coordinated. These will weave into existing and future infrastructure in order to ensure that the 
PDA Area is accessible and inviting from all approaches. The four streets surrounding the Phase A Project 
will each have a unique character, as further outlined below. The PDA Master Plan will create a cohesive 
network of streets, walking paths, bicycle paths and bike stations, and green connections. 
● Western Ave - Western Avenue is expected to be the primary arrival point for the PDA Area. Western 
Avenue is intended to prioritize transit service and low-stress bikeways, and to provide a thoughtfully 
designed pedestrian realm. The southern edge of Western Avenue will be activated by the hotel lobby, retail 
and restaurant, and the conference center with its corresponding open space. At the center of the Phase A 
PDA Area’s Western Avenue frontage, pedestrians will be welcomed into a project laneway that leads south 
to the Project Greenway. 
● Cattle Drive - Cattle Drive, running north-south, will serve as a “Main Street” for the PDA Area, 
designed to incorporate vehicles, transit, cycling, and an active pedestrian realm. Building lobbies, retail 
and restaurant and other active uses will also provide active ground floor frontage along Cattle Drive, while 
loading areas and service access will be reduced to a minimum along this neighborhood main street, with 
the exception of the primary loading dock entrance for the hotel and residential buildings in the Phase A 
Project, which will be located in the first block of the street. This careful consideration of ground floor use 
and streetscape design will help activate the north-bound pedestrian promenade and adjoining street rooms. 
Expanded frontage zones, referred to as “street rooms”, will further enrich and expand the pedestrian 
experience and reciprocity between buildings and the public realm along Cattle Drive. Eventually, Cattle 
Drive will be an important pedestrian and low-stress bicycle connector down to Cambridge Street and 
beyond to the anticipated future multimodal West Station. 
● East Drive - East Drive, also running north-south, will be an important connector for vehicular traffic. 
It incorporates street parking, as well as a potential transit service stop. The lab/office building will 
incorporate active ground floor uses at the street level and together with the conference center frames the 
Project Greenway. East Drive will also feature low-stress bikeways and a thoughtfully designed pedestrian 
realm. 
● DEF Drive - DEF Drive completes the Phase A Project perimeter and will primarily be a street 
providing access to the existing DEF, the Phase A Project’s single underground parking garage entry, and 
consolidated loading and services for the lab/office buildings.

In addition to generous sidewalks and low-stress bikeways on Western Avenue, Cattle Drive, and East

 5.3 Public Realm 
The PDA Master Plan will create an open and inviting public realm that aims to connect Allston residents 
with new employees, residents, and visitors of the Proposed Project, along with the Harvard community 
and others. A primary objective of the open space plan is to create an environment that is open and inviting 
to the public. Through a range of engaging publicly-accessible spaces, the Proposed Project seeks to 
establish strong connections with existing amenities, build upon completed portions of the open space 
network, and advance towards a future continuous open space connecting the Honan-Allston Public Library 
to Soldiers Field Road and toward the Charles River. 
The Phase A Project includes approximately 2.9 acres of Publicly Accessible Open Space and Public Realm 
areas within the developable portion of the PDA Area as illustrated on Exhibit D. 
 5.3.1 Streetscape Improvements 
The PDA Master Plan will create a cohesive network of streets, walking paths, bicycle paths and bike 
stations, and green connections. Western Avenue will be upgraded to prioritize transit and will be made to 
be pedestrian- and bike-friendly. Western Avenue is also anticipated to serve as a primary access point for 
motorized vehicles entering and exiting the PDA Area. 
Street planning guidelines for the PDA Area provide for elements which are necessary to create a cohesive 
and sustainable public realm. Principles follow those of Boston’s Complete Streets Guidelines, which state 
that streets should be sensitive to their context, recognized as an essential component of publicly-accessible 
open spaces, supportive of multiple functions, and encouraging of non-motorized uses. Publicly accessible 

 
 
12 
streets will shape the PDA Area physical setting and public realm. Plans should enhance the quality of the 
public realm to create great streets and memorable places. 
Following guidance from Boston’s Complete Streets Guidelines, the street and sidewalk configuration will 
ensure high performance and longevity for the investment in new street trees. Pervious paving and 
structural soil volumes in the planted areas provide horticultural support for the trees, but they also 
significantly increase infiltration and reduce the outflow of stormwater in rain events through below-grade 
detention. Over time, this system should ensure a notable increase in canopy coverage throughout the area 
and will contribute to the evolution of a unified network of streets throughout. 
A coherent pedestrian realm that comprises a diverse urban landscape will be achieved over time. Critical 
ingredients include the organization of buildings, land uses, and memorable spaces that contribute to a 
unique urban quality; activation of the street with extensive programs of public accommodation; and the 
efficient and systematic design of vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian ways. Boston’s Complete Streets 
Guidelines offer guidance on programmatic issues, dimensions, materials and techniques, performance and 
function, and the achievement of comprehensive environmental benefits. In order to provide the best 
pedestrian realm, curb cuts on main streets will be minimized. 
● 
Pedestrian Zone: Sidewalks are planned to have continuous and unobstructed pathways and sight 
lines. Uniform, consistent surfaces are recommended and will be made with poured concrete surface or 
smooth pavers that utilize large dimensions. Any material other than poured concrete should be reviewed 
and approved by the Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities. The pedestrian zone will line up 
legibly and logically with intersection crosswalks. This system achieves optimal navigation and ease of 
travel for persons with varying disabilities. 
● 
Furnishing Zone: Between the pedestrian zone and the curb of the roadbed, a furnishing zone is 
contemplated to accommodate tree planting and soil infiltration zones, pedestrian and street lighting, street 
furniture, and any fixtures and appurtenances required for transit. Locations and dimensions will vary 
according to specific conditions and roadway configuration, but throughout the PDA Area, this zone is 
envisioned to be 4 to 6 feet in width, plus curb extensions where they exist. By using unit pavers, the 
furnishing zones will have permeability for stormwater infiltration. 
● 
Frontage Zone: The frontage zone will frame the inside edge of the pedestrian zone, extend the 
sidewalk as dimensions allow, and may accommodate sidewalk cafes, store entries, retail displays, and 
landscape elements. The frontage zone can be widened to create plazas and gathering spaces at periodic 
breaks in the street wall. Dimensions and materials in the frontage will vary according to building use and 
building type. 
Given the phased nature of the build-out of the PDA Area, interim roadway and sidewalk improvements 
may be located from time to time on portions of the PDA Area that have not been redeveloped as 
contemplated by the PDA Master Plan. Such interim roadway and sidewalk improvements shall be subject 
to review and approval by BTD as part of the applicable construction management plan, and any temporary 
roads/access shall be designed to facilitate multimodal safety and connectivity in a manner that is informed 
by and does not preclude implementation of subsequent phased development of the PDA Master Plan. 
 5.3.2 Open Space 
The Phase A Project includes approximately 2.9 acres of Publicly Accessible Open Space and Public Realm 
areas within the developable portion of the PDA Area as illustrated on Exhibit D, which will be developed 

 
 
13 
and maintained by the Proponent or Harvard and will be available for use by residents, tenants, workers, 
visitors, hotel and conference center guests, and the general public. The open space network will also 
promote forward-thinking stormwater management and resiliency best practices. 
Landscape is an important element which helps to define the character of the PDA Area. The building 
placement and the landscape design will work together to provide form and definition to the Phase A 
Project’s Publicly Accessible Open Space. This PDA Master Plan establishes a network of open spaces and 
increased landscape areas along Cattle Drive which will help to make Cattle Drive an important pedestrian 
destination. It will also enhance landscape function to minimize the impact on ecosystems and water 
resources, reduce drainage impacts of projects, and improve the quality of stormwater management. 
The Proposed Project’s Publicly Accessible Open Space areas include the Project Greenway, a laneway 
connecting Western Avenue to the Project Greenway, as well as smaller planned “sidewalk room” open 
space areas. The sidewalk rooms are areas intended to provide open space where there would otherwise be 
private enclosed space, creating Publicly Accessible Open Space areas that provide greenery, art or other 
visual and physical amenities and pockets of resting space on alternating sides of Cattle Drive. 
The City of Boston’s Imagine Boston 2030 plan commits to investing in new open spaces in areas of new 
housing and job growth, as well as developing family- and kid-friendly environments that promote 
opportunities to play everywhere. The Proposed Project will help increase the area’s open space ratio and 
follow the plan’s goals of envisioning and creating an accessible open space system, enhancing the urban 
natural environment, and improving quality of life and well-being in the city. 
As used in this PDA Master Plan, (1) “Publicly Accessible Open Space” shall mean and include, as 
applicable, hardscape and greenscape areas, parks, playgrounds, active sports and recreation and court 
areas, passive recreation areas, plazas, benches and sitting areas, greens and lawns, wooded, natural, and 
wetland areas, and pedestrian and bicycle paths and walkways; provided that (x) in each case such areas 
are publicly accessible, open to the sky, and accessible from grade spaces that are also publicly accessible, 
(y) sidewalks (other than sidewalks that run within or along the boundary of Publicly Accessible Open

and pedestrian bicycle paths), buffer areas between buildings and roadbed/curbline, greened medians that 
provide pedestrian scale on the streets, connections, and/or walkways through private parcel sites that 
provide connections to amenities available to the public, or through-block connections, and retail-associated 
space (in leases or not), including outdoor seating areas serving retail, restaurant, bar and entertainment

Publicly Accessible Open Space areas to be constructed as part of the Proposed Project, subject to review

5.3.3 Utilities 
 
The PDA Master Plan will involve the construction of water, sewer and storm drainage facilities in

 5.3.4 Sustainability 
The Proposed Project will demonstrate best practices that promote sustainability, including measures to 
reduce carbon emissions from building construction and operations and use of renewable resources. In 
addition to complying with the requirements of Article 37 (Green Buildings) of the Zoning Code, the 
Proposed Project will be based on a series of sustainability objectives, including: 
● 
Reduce vulnerability to climate change impacts including natural hazards by integrating climate 
change adaptation into planning and project design; 

 
 
15 
● 
Promote health, productivity, and safety of the community through design and maintenance of the 
built environment; 
● 
Enhance the health of ecosystems and increase the diversity of native species; 
● 
Establish indicators for sustainability that will enable monitoring, reporting and continuous 
improvement; 
● 
Minimize the impact on ecosystems and water resources, and reduce drainage impacts of the 
Proposed Project; 
● 
Promote smart use of water, inside and out, to reduce potable water consumption; 
● 
Minimize greenhouse gas emissions by targeting zero net carbon building performance and 
including low carbon building design and engineering strategies, and procuring renewable electricity; 
● 
Prioritizing, as feasible, the use of low carbon building materials, especially for building structure 
and enclosure systems, and managing construction operations minimize carbon emissions and reduce waste; 
● 
Promote better indoor air quality and access to daylight and views; 
● 
Promote efficient, sustainable transportation options and open space; 
● 
Emphasize walkable mixed-use neighborhoods with good connections to nearby communities; and 
● 
Reduce the environmental consequences of the construction and operation of buildings and 
infrastructure.

The Proposed Project will generate housing and jobs linkage funds for the City of Boston, as 
required by Section 80B-7(3)(a) of the Code, in accordance with a Master Development Impact Project 
Agreement to be executed by the Proponent and the BPDA (the “Master DIP Agreement”), and individual 
Development Impact Project Agreements to effectuate the terms of the Master DIP Agreement that shall be 
executed by the owner of each building containing Development Impact Uses prior to issuance of the 
building permit for such building, and paid in connection with the construction and operation of each such 
building. The Housing Contribution Grant rate and the Jobs Contribution Grant rate shall be $13.00 and 
$2.39 per square foot of Gross Floor Area of Development Impact Uses in the Phase A Project, subject to 
an exception for the first 100,000 square feet of Gross Floor Area of Development Impact Project Uses in 
the Proposed Project. 
 6.3 
Workforce, Economic Development, and Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Benefits 
 
● 
The Phase A Project is expected to create approximately 2,300 permanent jobs relating to the 
commercial, hotel, retail, restaurant, parking and residential administration components, and to create 
approximately 2,000 construction jobs in a variety of trades. 
● 
Historically there have been disparities in economic opportunities available to under-represented 
populations in the commercial real estate industry, particularly for wealth creation opportunities and true 
ownership of institutional-scale development projects. With regard to the capitalization of the Phase A 
Project, the Proponent set out to raise investment from Black and Latinx investors for a targeted 5% of 
equity for the Phase A Project. Through concerted and wide-ranging efforts to identify, source, and 
structure such investments, the Proponent was able to bring over 150 Black and Latinx individuals into the 
Phase A Project’s equity ownership, including local Boston-area residents, in amounts that totaled 

 
 
17 
approximately $30 million. This represents what is believed to be the largest such inclusionary investor 
initiative (in terms of total dollars) for a private development in the history of the City of Boston. The 
Proponent intends to provide for similar inclusionary equity ownership as part of the Phase B Project. 
● 
To foster small, local, MBE, and/or WBE retailers, the Proponent is committed to allocating 25% 
of the retail at the Phase A Project to such retailers, and, as necessary, work with such retailers to provide 
advantageous lease terms. 
● 
As part of the Proponent’s commitment to allocate approximately 25% of the retail at the Phase A 
Project to small, local, MBE, and/or WBE retailers, the Proponent will designate a ~1,500 SF ground floor 
retail space in the Phase A Project as a flexible arts space that will include a rotating program of art and 
cultural uses, which could include pop up gallery opportunities for local artists to show their work. 
● 
The Proponent has committed to awarding at least 15% of the total value of its preconstruction 
contracts for the Proposed Project to certified MBE and WBE firms and to awarding at least 15% of the 
total value of its construction contracts for the Proposed Project to certified MBE and WBE firms. 
 6.4 
Sustainable and Resilient Development 
 
● 
The Proposed Project will advance Boston’s carbon neutral and climate ready goals by 
incorporating a variety of sustainable design and resilient building strategies that will reduce carbon 
emissions, improve water quality, reduce the urban heat island effect, maximize the conservation of energy 
and water, and reduce the risk of flooding due to sea level rise. 
● 
The lab/office, residential and hotel buildings of the Phase A Project will be eligible to receive 
LEED Gold certification at a minimum using the LEEDv4 rating system, exceeding the City’s requirements 
under Article 37 - Green Buildings. The Phase A Project lab/office, residential and hotel buildings will be 
eligible to achieve Fitwel certification (a certification system focused on building health for all, originally 
created by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and U.S. General Services Administration) 
in addition to LEED Gold certification. 
● 
The Phase A Project will reduce energy and stationary source GHG emissions by targeting zero net 
carbon building performance including a 40% reduction in carbon emissions as compared to the Base Case 
(Stretch Code) with 2035 electric grid emissions. 
● 
The Phase A Project will prioritize systems and solutions that utilize renewable energy, and will 
explore the feasibility of providing 90% of the Proposed Phase A Lab/Office and Hotel and 100% of the 
Residential and Conference Center building energy needs by electricity when the Proposed Phase A Project 
opens. Additionally, the Proposed Phase A Project will achieve a BERDO emissions standard of 1 kg 
co2e/sf/yr, and will explore a reduction below this level. 
● 
The Phase A Project will utilize a combination of on-site renewable energy and utilities provided 
through the District Energy Facility in connection with the Conference Center, if feasible. 
● 
The Proposed Project will consider incorporating design strategies and construction materials to 
reduce Heat Island conditions, where feasible, including the use of low SRI building wall and roof products 
and site hardscape materials, building and site canopies, and landscape design and plantings. 

 
 
18 
● 
The Proposed Project will incorporate design elements to improve on-site stormwater management 
and reduce risk of precipitation-based flooding. The Proposed Project will provide a significant amount of 
public realm and open space improvements, and the Proposed Project will be designed and engineered to 
manage the 32-year storm (6.7 inches of rainfall), exceeding Boston Water and Sewer Commission 
(BWSC) requirements and will prioritize the use of green infrastructure solutions. 
● 
The PDA Area is not within a current FEMA floodplain, and is located outside the boundary for 
the 2070 1% annual chance event used in Climate Ready Boston. While the Proposed Project has limited 
coastal flood risk, first floor elevations are proposed to be raised to 18.5-19.5 feet Boston City Base (BCB). 
● 
The Proponent will provide updated individual building Article 37 Initial Filings including updated 
performance models for review and approval by the IGBC. 
 6.5 
Smart Utilities 
 
● 
The Phase A Project has completed a district energy microgrid feasibility assessment and master 
plan, and reviewed the results with the BPDA. The study included analysis of an ambient water loop served 
by a combination of air to water heat pumps, ground source and electric boilers in incremental steps to 
reduce natural gas consumption in buildings for heating and domestic hot water demands. 
 
● 
The Phase A Project has assessed the necessary infrastructure improvements for telecom conduit 
and a utilidor, including confirmation of adequate system capacity for the Proposed Project, and 
coordination of service connection locations, and necessary approvals. 
 
● 
The Proposed Project will provide for stormwater resiliency storage to accommodate an additional 
1.5 inches of runoff, above the typically-required 1.25-inch water quality volume, for the impervious site 
areas of the Proposed Project. Those volumes result in a total of 2.75-inches of stormwater storage for the 
Proposed Project. 
 
● 
The Phase A Project has assessed the needs for additional conduit for future electric and fiber 
infrastructure in relevant sidewalks, to support the City’s needs for deployment of future smart technology 
(with such review to be coordinated with the Public Improvement Commission). 
 
● 
The Phase A Project will comply with the City of Boston EV Readiness Policy for New 
Developments, including EV chargers and needed infrastructure. Twenty-five percent (25%) of the 
Proposed Project’s parking spaces will be EVSE-Installed; and the remaining seventy five percent (75%) 
of parking spaces will be EV-Ready for future installation, in each case to the extent required by the City 
of Boston EV Readiness Policy. Transformers have been sized to accommodate anticipated future loads. 
 
● 
The Proponent will prepare a utility site plan showing the infrastructure described in the bullets 
above, as well as all other relevant utility infrastructure, including water, sewer, drainage, gas, electric (for 
buildings and for street lights), telecom, transformers, and gas meters. All lateral connections to the 
proposed buildings are to be installed in conjunction with the development of roadways and other necessary 
infrastructure to ensure there will be no additional street openings as the project moves forward. 
 
● 
The Phase A Project will prepare a plan to address relevant conflicts reported through the City of 
Boston Utility Coordination System (COBUCS). 
 
 6.6 
Traffic and Transit Benefits 

 
 
19 
 
● The Proposed Project will introduce transportation improvements for a wide range of users, including 
new multimodal connections that currently do not exist. Those connections, such as an east-west shared-
use path (and Project Greenway) and complete streets, will connect pedestrians and bicyclists traveling 
through and to the PDA Area from surrounding neighborhoods. The Proposed Project will prioritize transit 
improvements and safe pedestrian and bicycling movements on Western Avenue. Final design of new and 
reconstructed roadways, including any and all pick up/drop off locations, is subject to further review and 
approval by the BPDA, BTD, and PIC. 
● Proposed transit mitigation measures include working with the MBTA to improve service on bus 
Routes 86 and 70, implementation of supplemental transit services, in cooperation with other Allston-area 
stakeholders, to provide connections to key transit hubs, and transit priority and bus stop improvements on 
Western Avenue. The service plan details for the neighborhood transit connections are expected to be 
determined in collaboration with the City of Boston and Allston-Brighton Transportation Management 
Association (ABTMA) via the Allston-Brighton Neighborhood Connector Study and with the MBTA via 
the Bus Network Redesign project. Those efforts will include broad input from residents and Allston-
Brighton stakeholders, the City, BPDA, and MBTA, as well as other developers in the area. 
● The Proponent is engaged in specific coordination with Harvard to develop a transit service plan that 
seeks to address the Phase A Project’s trip demand to/from Harvard Square, as well as Harvard University’s 
own needs. 
● The Proponent will include a total of 600 bike parking spaces within the Phase A Project, distributed 
across indoor and outdoor locations and in compliance with the City’s Bike Parking Guidelines. 
● Two Bluebike stations will be installed by the City in connection with the completion of the Phase A 
Project (at locations to be jointly approved by the Proponent and the City). Each such station will 
accommodate approximately 23 docks. Consistent with the City’s Bike Share program, a financial 
contribution of $250,000.00 will be made to the Boston Transportation Department not later than the date 
the Phase A Project obtains its first Certificate of Occupancy. Installation of both stations is anticipated to 
be completed concurrently with substantial completion of the Phase A Project. No other payment will be 
required in connection with the City’s Bike Parking program or implementation. 
● To support needed transit improvements, the Proponent will work with the BPDA, BTD, and the MBTA 
to design and install an eastbound transit lane on Western Avenue directly fronting the Phase A PDA Area. 
Final design requires BPDA, BTD, and MBTA approval. Installation is anticipated to be completed 
concurrently with substantial completion of the Phase A Project. 
● To further support transit improvements for the Phase A Project, and in support of larger transit 
improvements for the Allston community, the Proponent and Harvard University will participate in, and 
the Proponent will provide financial support to the BPDA in the amount of $500,000 for, a holistic study 
and design effort of a “Western Avenue Transitway” which will prioritize transit use, low stress bikeways, 
and generous pedestrian accommodations. This effort will allow the BPDA and BTD to advance work to 
support transit operations that will experience increased demand, and is in line with efforts underway by 
the BPDA through the Western Avenue Corridor Rezoning Study. The Proponent’s financial contribution 
will be made in two installments: the first installment, in the amount of $250,000, will be due concurrently 
with the issuance of a building permit for the Phase A Project; and the second installment, also in the amount 
of $250,000, will be due concurrently with substantial completion of the Phase A Project.

In connection with the development of the Proposed Project in accordance with this PDA Master Plan, the

10.0 
Effect of PDA Master Plan 
 
 10.1 Zoning 
The PDA Area is located within the Allston Landing North Economic Development Area, which is 
governed by Article 51 of the Zoning Code. As shown on the Survey, Exhibit B, the PDA Area contains 
more than five acres of land, and since it is not located in a residential zoning district, treating this 
submission as a Master Plan is authorized by Article 3-1A.a of the Zoning Code. 
This PDA Master Plan sets forth the zoning for all elements of the Proposed Project for the PDA Area. 
Upon approval by the BPDA and the Boston Zoning Commission, any PDA Development Plan for a 
Proposed Project within the PDA Area that is consistent with this PDA Master Plan will be presumed to be 
consistent with underlying zoning and all other provisions of the Zoning Code to the extent that such 
requirements are made applicable and have been addressed in this PDA Master Plan or a subsequent PDA 
Development Plan. A Certification of Consistency for individual buildings described in this PDA Master 
Plan shall be issued pursuant to Section 80C-8 of the Zoning Code, in the case of Proponent’s buildings, or 
in the case of the Conference Center, under the provisions of Section 80D-10 of the Zoning Code. 
 9.2 
Parcels 
The PDA Area is an assembly of various legal lots which were acquired by Harvard over a period of time. 
In order to implement the Proposed Project, it is contemplated that new legal lots will be created and that 
one or more of those lots may be leased or conveyed to third parties. A plan of the proposed parcels is 
shown on Exhibit J attached hereto. This plan shows the proposed locations of each building and open 
space with respect to streets, and intended dimensions land area for each parcel, which are subject to 
modification as set forth in this PDA Master Plan. 
Notwithstanding that lots may be in separate legal ownership and separated by streets, the dimensional 
requirements and Floor Area Ratio set forth in this PDA Master Plan shall apply to the PDA Area as a 
whole and not to each individual lot, and a Certification of Consistency may be issued for each separate 
building and/or separately for each of the Phase A Project and the Phase B Project; provided that non-
compliance by a particular building or phase shall not affect compliance by any other currently existing 
building or a building for which a Certification of Consistency has been issued. 
 9.3 
Development Review 
Each building component of the Proposed Project within the PDA Area will undergo review as required by 
Article 80 of the Zoning Code, as well as design review subsequent to the submission of one or more PDA 

 
 
22 
Development Plans for the Proposed Project. Review of environmental impacts will be studied during the 
Article 80-B Large Project Review process, taking into account the technical studies already performed. 
Among other matters, transportation impacts will be updated as needed if the Proposed Project is not 
consistent with the building envelope and program uses studied in the Transportation Impact Study. 
The design of the individual buildings will be subject to review by the Boston Civic Design Commission 
and the Boston Interagency Green Building Committee in accordance with Article 28 and Article 37 of the 
Code, respectively, and to further review by the BPDA of the schematic design, design development and 
construction drawings, pursuant to the BPDA's Development Review Guidelines and Article 80B and 
Article 37 of the Code. Each individual building shall meet the City’s requirements in effect at the time of 
submission of the individual building design review filing respecting updates to Article 37, USGBC’s 
LEED Rating Systems, and Boston Climate Resiliency and Sea Level Rise Base Flood Elevation 
requirements, Climate Action Plan or their successors. Aspects of the Proposed Project may also require 
approvals of other governmental agencies, such as the City of Boston's Public Improvement Commission 
and the Boston Conservation Commission. No permits for any elements of the Proposed Project included 
in this PDA Master Plan, as the same may be amended, shall be required from the Zoning Board of Appeals. 
In addition, each of the Phases and the buildings and improvements to be incorporated in them, will be 
subject to one or more PDA Development Plans submitted and approved in accordance with Article 80C 
of the Code. Note that these regulations may evolve over the timespan of project review and approval. Any 
proposed buildings and/or PDA Development Plans will be required to comply with the governing 
regulations in effect at the time of approval.

Dimensional Requirements and Urban Design Parameters 
 
In addition to other requirements, the PDA Master Plan’s development will be subject to the following 
additional dimensional requirements and urban design parameters: 
 
(i) 
Maximum Building Coverage. The portion of the land area within the PDA Area that is 
occupied by the footprint of buildings shall not exceed 50% in the aggregate, for purposes of 
which all buildings within the PDA Area shall be taken into account, and compared against the 
entire land area of the PDA Area, including without limitation open space and roadways. In 
calculating the portion of land area that is occupied by the footprint of buildings, a building 
footprint shall not include areas located wholly below grade or below open space, roadways, 
courtyards, service areas, and/or other similar areas open to the sky. 
 
(ii) 
Active Uses. Designs for each building shall, to the extent possible, seek to maximize the 
storefront area used for Active Uses (as defined below) on building facades facing on Western 
Avenue and East, Cattle and Science Drives as determined through the BPDA design review 
process. As used in this PDA Master Plan, “Active Uses” shall mean building lobbies, 
conference center uses and any of the following other uses if located on the ground floor: 
Restaurant Uses; Retail Uses; Hotel Uses; Facility of Public Assembly Uses; Neighborhood 
Medical Uses; Educational Uses, Art Uses; Entertainment Uses; Institutional Uses (as outlined 
and limited above); Community and Cultural Uses; and uses accessory thereto, in each case as 
outlined on Exhibit E. 
 
(iii) 
Parking, Service and Loading Dock Entrances; Private Service Driveways. For each 
building, dimensions and locations of curb cuts for parking entrances shall be determined 
through the BPDA design review process. 
 
(iv) 
Façade and Horizontal Building Wall Designs. Designs for each building, including horizontal 
facade massing, shall be determined through the BPDA design review process, as part of which 
buildings facades should be designed to maximize visual interest and avoid being perceived as a 
solid uninterrupted horizontal wall using publicly accessible ground-floor through-openings, or 
other such design features, or by being visually articulated as several smaller masses using 
different materials or colors, vertical breaks, bays, or other architectural elements. In addition, 
buildings should reflect a rhythm and variation appropriate to the urban context. 
 
Any variations from the use and dimensional requirements and urban design parameters set forth above and 
in Section 4.3 shall require approval pursuant to the PDA Development Plan, and for material variations may 
also require an amendment to this PDA Master Plan and the applicable PDA Development Plan, as 
determined by the BPDA.

I. 
Proponent 
Tishman Speyer ERC Developer, L.L.C. 
II. 
Project 
Location 
The PDA Area is an approximately 14.2 acre parcel of land, bounded generally by 
Western Avenue on the north, the Harvard property which is ground-leased to 
National Resilience Inc. on the east, the Harvard University District Energy Facility 
(“DEF”) on the southeast, and Harvard property west of Hague Street on the west. 
III. 
Development 
 Concept 
The PDA Master Plan proposes the construction of multiple buildings that comprise 
Phase A of the Proposed Project, containing a total of approximately 900,000 square 
feet and described conceptually below: 
 
● an office/lab building with approximately 440,000 square feet of office/lab and 
retail and restaurant space, 
● a residential structure having two distinct massings with approximately 
263,500 square feet of residential and retail and restaurant space and 
approximately 345 units, 
● a hotel with approximately 135,000 square feet of hotel and retail space and 
approximately 250 hotel rooms, 
● an approximately 61,500 square foot conference center and retail and 
restaurant space, and 
● up to 580 off-street parking spaces. 
 
The PDA Master Plan also includes various open spaces, including a greenway that 
will bisect the site (the “Project Greenway”). 
 
Those spaces will connect to the west to the network of open spaces beginning 
behind the Honan-Allston Branch Library at Ray Mellone Park and extending 
eastward through Rena Park and continuing east to Soldiers Field Road. 
 
In addition, the PDA Master Plan provides for new roadways and access driveways. 
The most significant of these is Cattle Drive, a new north-south roadway which will 
provide access into and through the PDA Area. In the long-term, Cattle Drive will 
provide a through connection from Western Avenue to Cambridge Street and on to 
the future multimodal West Station commuter rail stop. 
 

 
 
 
EAST\183845827.44 
IV. 
 Project Uses 
Allowed uses for the PDA Area include, among others, office, laboratory, 
residential, cultural, research and development, service, open space (including 
programmed open space), hotel, conference center, and retail and/or restaurant, 
together with accessory and ancillary uses thereto. A limited amount of 
Institutional Uses will be allowed in the Proposed Project, consistent with 
applicable Institutional Master Plan requirements. Uses will also include below-
grade, at-grade, and structured accessory parking for all types of uses as set forth 
in the "Parking" section of the PDA Master Plan. Roadways constructed within 
the PDA Area are expected to serve the PDA uses and adjacent uses, including 
institutional uses. There will also be below-grade utility lines running from the 
DEF to institutional and non-institutional buildings in the vicinity. 
 
 
V. 
Public Benefits 
The development of the Proposed Project contemplated by the PDA Master Plan will 
provide a range of public benefits, including: 
● Increased and improved publicly-accessible open space which connects to a 
broader network of open spaces; 
● New affordable housing units in connection with any residential development 
that comply with City requirements; 
● Housing and job linkage payments from qualifying uses in connection with 
construction of buildings containing such uses; 
● New construction and permanent jobs; 
● Increased tax revenues for the City; 
● Measures to advance Boston’s carbon neutral and climate ready goals by 
incorporating a variety of sustainable design and resilient building strategies 
that will reduce carbon emissions, improve water quality, reduce the urban 
heat island effect, maximize the conservation of energy and water, and reduce 
the risk of flooding due to sea level rise; 
● Measures to promote diversity, equity and inclusion, including the creation of 
investment opportunities for diverse investors, commitments to contract with 
MBE and WBE firms for 15% of the total value of preconstruction and 
construction contracts, and initiatives to allocate 25% of the retail to small, 
local, MBE, and/or WBE retailers, and 
● Transportation improvements, including new complete streets and transit 
service serving both persons living and working at the Proposed Project and 
the general public in the Allston community. 
 
Public benefits associated with each phase of the Proposed Project will be 
included in the PDA Development Plan for such phase.

Exhibit D and include, among others, office, laboratory, residential, cultural, research and 
development, service, open space (including programmed open space), hotel, conference center, 
and retail and/or restaurant, together with Accessory and Ancillary Uses. The conference center is 
anticipated to be owned and operated by Harvard as provided in Harvard’s 2013 Institutional 
Master Plan (as the same may be amended). In addition, a limited amount of additional Institutional 
Uses (that do not constitute High Impact Subuses under the Zoning Code) will be allowed in the

set forth in the "Proposed Parking and Loading Facilities" section of this Development Plan. 
Roadways constructed within the Project Site are expected to serve the Project uses and adjacent 
uses, including institutional uses. There will also be below-grade utility lines running from the 
DEF to institutional and non-institutional buildings in the vicinity. Other than as specified in this 
Development Plan or the Master Plan, the only use regulations applicable to the Project Site Area 
are those set forth in this paragraph and Exhibit D. 
It is anticipated that construction of the Project will be phased, and the construction of the 
Project’s structures containing residential, hotel and conference center uses are anticipated to be 
commenced within approximately six (6) months of the commencement of the Project’s office/lab 
building. In addition, the portion of the Project Greenway within the Project is anticipated to be 
substantially complete within six (6) months following completion of the Project’s office/lab 
building, and Public Realm and Publicly Accessible Open Space areas associated with each 
building within the Project are anticipated to be substantially complete within six (6) months 
following completion of such building, in all cases subject to seasonal conditions. Some portions 
of the Project Site may be used from time to time as construction laydown and staging areas, or 
for infrastructure uses such as stormwater management.

Proposed Open Spaces and Landscaping. The Project will include the 
establishment of significant areas of open space on the Project Site. As currently designed, the 
Project is anticipated to create approximately 2.9 acres of open space, including Publicly 
Accessible Open Space and Public Realm areas. The central focal point of the Project’s open 
space will be an approximately-1.4-acre portion of the publicly accessible greenway area intended 
to eventually connect the Honan-Allston Library and the Allston neighborhood all the way to the 
Charles River (such portion is referred to herein as the “Project Greenway”), as well as a project 
laneway through which pedestrians will be welcomed from the center of the Project Site’s Western 
Avenue frontage, south to the Project Greenway. The Project Greenway will be actively 

 
 
5 
 
 
programmed with a wide variety of events and activities. The Proponent envisions that the Project 
Greenway will provide a vibrant, dynamic, and activated public space that will benefit the local 
Allston community, as well as the greater Boston area. The design guidelines attached hereto as 
Exhibit F include provisions addressing the public realm to be developed as part of the Project, 
including the Project Greenway. 
In addition to the Project Greenway, various laneways within the Project Site will create 
an intimate, porous urban environment that welcomes pedestrians and will contain diverse 
elements including programmed greenspaces, landscaped plazas, and dynamic public art 
installations. The public realm improvements proposed for the Project are intended to create new 
connections, including for users such as Allston residents, students and faculty of Harvard, and 
new employees, residents, and visitors of the Project. Through a range of inviting and engaging 
Publicly Accessible Open Spaces and Public Realm areas, including the Project Greenway, the 
Project is planned with the goal of establishing strong connections with existing communities and 
to be the first phase of a future connection from the existing Allston neighborhood to Soldiers 
Field Road and the Charles River. 
Publicly Accessible Open Space and Public Realm areas to be constructed as part of the 
Project, subject to completion of BPDA design review, consist of the following: 
• Project Greenway – The Project Greenway will create a new east-west Publicly Accessible 
Open Space destination for surrounding communities, and will bolster the area’s connective, 
pedestrian fabric. This portion of the open space network will serve as a multi-constituency, 
multi-seasonal focal point of public realm space and programming. The Project Greenway 
design will be flexible and able to accommodate unique seasonal programs and events. While 
remaining open and flexible, the Project Greenway will contribute a significant landscape 
presence through a robust canopy, plantings, and visible green infrastructure where possible 
and appropriate. 
 
• Laneway - A new Publicly Accessible Open Space laneway connecting Western Avenue 
directly to the Project Greenway, at the heart of the Project Site, will be located between the 
Treehouse Conference Center described in the Master Plan, and the residential and hotel 
buildings. The laneway will be designed with a distinctly urban character, surrounded by active 
ground floor uses and lobby entrances. Canopy trees and other site elements will define and 
direct circulation between the different programs and establish a clear primary path between 
Western Avenue and the Project Greenway. 
 
• Street Rooms - A series of Publicly Accessible Open Space “street rooms” are intended along 
Cattle Drive to provide expanded areas adjacent to sidewalks for greenery, art or other visual 
and physical amenities. They provide alternating pockets of resting space on opposite sides of

7. 
Transportation. The key vehicular access point to the Project Site is from Western 
Avenue via two proposed new roadways, currently named Cattle Drive and East Drive (with final 
names of roadways to be determined in connection with the review process for the streets 
administered by the Public Improvement Commission). Those new roadways, together with DEF 
Drive, will be constructed by Harvard or its affiliates as part of the Master Project, and are shown 
on Exhibit C. Western Avenue is connected to the regional highway network via Soldiers Field 
Road to the east. The Project Site has indirect access to Interstate-90 (I-90) via offsite ramps on 
Cambridge Street south of the Project Site. In addition to the primary access from the north via 
Western Avenue, the Project Site will also be accessible from the south via an extension of Cattle 
Drive to Almy Street/Windom Street, which connects to Cambridge Street. Generous sidewalks 
and low-stress bikeways on Western Avenue, Cattle Drive, and East Drive will enhance pedestrian 
and bicycle movement through the Project Site. Western Avenue is expected to be the primary 
arrival point for the Project Site and is intended to prioritize transit service and low-stress 
bikeways, to include a pick-up/ drop-off lane, and to provide a thoughtfully designed pedestrian 
realm. The Project will be supported by plaza spaces, a shared-use path running east-west, and a 
laneway connecting Western Avenue to the central Project Greenway. 
Transit access to the Project will be provided by the existing MBTA Route 64, 66, 70, and 
86 buses. The Proponent will become a member of the Allston-Brighton TMA. Other proposed 
transit mitigation measures include working with the MBTA to improve service on bus Routes 86 
and 70, implementation of supplemental transit services, in cooperation with other Allston-area 
stakeholders, to provide connections to key transit hubs, and transit priority and bus stop 
improvements on Western Avenue and other corridors. The service plan details for the 
neighborhood transit connections are expected to be determined in collaboration with the City of 

 
 
7 
 
 
Boston and Allston-Brighton Transportation Management Association (ABTMA) via the Allston-
Brighton Neighborhood Connector Study and with the MBTA via the Bus Network Redesign 
project. These efforts will include broad input from residents and Allston-Brighton stakeholders, 
the City, BPDA, and MBTA, as well as other developers in the area. The Proponent is engaged in 
specific coordination with Harvard to develop a transit service plan that seeks to address the 
Project’s trip demand to/from Harvard Square, as well as Harvard University’s own needs. 
The Proponent has agreed to enter into a Master Transportation Access Plan Agreement 
(“TAPA”) for the Project with the Boston Transportation Department (“BTD”) specifying traffic 
mitigation, transportation improvements and transportation demand management (“TDM”) 
measures consistent with the Master Plan and this Development Plan that are required for the 
Project, prior to the issuance of the first building permit for a building in the Project. The Master 
TAPA shall provide that, prior to the commencement or construction of each building in the 
Project, and prior to the issuance of a Certification of Compliance and a Certification of 
Consistency, the owner of the applicable building may enter into a TAPA for such building with 
the BTD specifying the traffic mitigation, transportation improvements, and TDM measures 
consistent with the Master Plan, this Development Plan and the Master TAPA that are required for 
such building.

Proposed Parking and Loading Facilities. The Project is expected to include no 
more than 580 permanent parking spaces, which are to include up to 300 below-grade off-street 
parking spaces, and an additional up to 280 off-street parking spaces to serve uses within the 
Project that will be provided within existing Harvard parking facilities (that are not regulated by 
this Development Plan) outside the Master Plan PDA Area or surface parking lots within the 
Master Plan PDA Area but outside the Project Site, subject to such 280 additional spaces being 
incorporated into parking facilities as part of future development of the portion of the Master Plan 
PDA Area outside the Project Site. The plans for Cattle Drive, East Drive and DEF Drive also 
call for approximately 40 on-street parking spaces, in addition to the 580 off-street parking spaces 
referenced above, supporting adjacent retail and active uses. Access to the below-grade parking 
garage is planned on the north side of DEF Drive. The use of valet operations in the below-grade 
parking facilities will optimize the number of functional parking spaces, and will also serve the 
hotel use. 
The Project will result in the creation of substantial new, on-site roadway improvements, 
as described above. Curbside use will be allocated to accommodate transit stops, passenger drop-
off/pick-up/valet needs, as well as limited loading zones (each building will include an appropriate 
off-street loading area) and parking. Consolidated building service and loading areas are planned 
for all buildings. Loading and service for the buildings in the southern portion of the Project Site 
will take place along DEF Drive. Loading for the building in the northern portion of the Project 
Site will take place off of Cattle Drive and East Drive. All regular loading and service activities 
will occur internally to the footprints of Project buildings. 
The Project’s parking and loading facilities shall be subject to design, environmental and 
other development review by the BPDA, and the aspects of the Project approved as part of such 
review shall be and are hereby deemed to be the required parking and loading applicable to the

 13.4 Sustainable and Resilient Development 
 
● 
The Project will advance Boston’s carbon neutral and climate ready goals by incorporating 
a variety of sustainable design and resilient building strategies that will reduce carbon emissions, 
improve water quality, reduce the urban heat island effect, maximize the conservation of energy 
and water, and reduce the risk of flooding due to sea level rise. 

 
 
12 
 
 
● 
The lab/office, residential and hotel buildings of the Project will be eligible to receive 
LEED Gold certification at a minimum using the LEEDv4 rating system, exceeding the City’s 
requirements under Article 37 - Green Buildings. The Project lab/office, residential and hotel 
buildings will be eligible to achieve Fitwel certification (a certification system focused on building 
health for all, originally created by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and U.S. 
General Services Administration) in addition to LEED Gold certification. 
● 
The Project will reduce energy and stationary source GHG emissions by targeting zero net 
carbon building performance including a 40% reduction in carbon emissions as compared to the 
Base Case (Stretch Code) with 2035 electric grid emissions. 
● 
The Project will prioritize systems and solutions that utilize renewable energy, and will 
explore the feasibility of providing 90% of the Project’s Lab/Office and Hotel and 100% of the 
Residential and Conference Center building energy needs by electricity when the Project opens. 
Additionally, the Project will achieve a BERDO emissions standard of 1 kg co2e/sf/yr, and will 
explore a reduction below this level. 
● 
The Project will utilize a combination of on-site renewable energy and utilities provided 
through the District Energy Facility in connection with the Conference Center, if feasible. 
● 
The Project will consider incorporating design strategies and construction materials to 
reduce Heat Island conditions, where feasible, including the use of low SRI building wall and roof 
products and site hardscape materials, building and site canopies, and landscape design and 
plantings. 
● 
The Proposed Project will incorporate design elements to improve on-site stormwater 
management and reduce risk of precipitation-based flooding. The Proposed Project will provide a 
significant amount of public realm and open space improvements, and the Proposed Project will 
be designed and engineered to manage the 32-year storm (6.7 inches of rainfall), exceeding Boston 
Water and Sewer Commission (BWSC) requirements and will prioritize the use of green 
infrastructure solutions. 
● 
The Project Site is not within a current FEMA floodplain, and is located outside the 
boundary for the 2070 1% annual chance event used in Climate Ready Boston. While the Project 
has limited coastal flood risk, first floor elevations are proposed to be raised to 18.5-19.5 feet 
Boston City Base (BCB).

The Proponent will provide updated individual building Article 37 Initial Filings including 
updated performance models for review and approval by the IGBC.

accordance with this Development Plan, the Proponent has worked closely with the BPDA to 
develop a Language Access Plan (the “LAP”) for the Project. Based on the BPDA’s Limited 
English Proficiency Assessment, Mandarin Chinese, Brazilian Portuguese, and Spanish have been 
identified by the BPDA as threshold languages for the Allston neighborhood. The LAP addresses 
requirements for translation of vital documents respecting the Project. In addition to LAP 
requirements, the Proponent has identified affected individuals who utilize Korean, Arabic and 
Russian and has provided translations of project Fact Sheets in these languages. 
 
15. 
Effect of the Development Plan. This Development Plan sets forth the zoning for 
all elements of the Project for the Project Site. This Development Plan is consistent with the 
Master Plan and is therefore presumed to be compliant and consistent with underlying zoning and 
all other provisions of the Code to the extent that such requirements have been addressed in this 
Development Plan. A Certification of Consistency for individual buildings described in this 
Development Plan shall be issued pursuant to Section 80C-8 of the Zoning Code, in the case of 
Proponent’s buildings, or in the case of the Conference Center, under the provisions of Section 
80D-10 of the Zoning Code. In accordance with Sections 80C-9 of the Code, the issuance of a 
Certification of Consistency or Partial Certification of Consistency pursuant to Section 80C-8 
confirms consistency of each applicable element of the Project with this Development Plan and 
constitutes compliance with the requirements of the Code to the extent such requirements have 
been addressed in this Development Plan. In order to implement the Project, new legal lots may 
be created and one or more may be leased or conveyed to be in separate ownership. 
Notwithstanding that legal lots may be in separate legal ownership and/or separated by streets 
the dimensional requirements set forth in this Development Plan (other than maximum heights 
of buildings) shall apply to the Project Site as a whole and not to each individual lot, and each 
separate building shall be eligible for and may receive a Certification of Consistency. 
Noncompliance of any building shall not affect compliance of any other building for which a 
Certificate of Consistency has been issued, or the right to construct any other building 
contemplated by this Development Plan. 
 
17. 
Amendment of Development Plan. Any owner of an individual lot within the 
Project Site may seek amendment of this Development Plan only as to such lot in accordance with 
the procedures prescribed by the Code without the consent of any other owner of land within the 
Project Site; provided, however, that no such amendment shall affect the rights or obligations of 
any other owner of land in the Project Site under this Development Plan or any agreements between 
the Proponent and the BPDA or other City agencies. Given the scope of the proposed Master 
Project, and in light of the various reviews necessary to secure all required permits and approvals, 
the Proponent may seek to make modifications to the buildings and site improvements included in 
the Project. Proposed minor modifications to individual buildings and site improvements may be 
approved by the BPDA as part of a staff-level review process, without requiring an amendment 
to this Development Plan, subject to the use and dimensional requirements and urban design 
parameters set forth in this Development Plan; provided that in no event may the total Gross Floor 
Area, the total Residential Gross Floor Area, or the total non-Residential Gross Floor Area within 

 
 
16 
 
 
the Project be increased or decreased by more than 10% without an amendment to this 
Development Plan as may be determined by the BPDA.

Dimensional Requirements and Urban Design Parameters 
 
In addition to other requirements, the Development Plan’s development will be subject to the 
following additional dimensional requirements and urban design parameters: 
 
(i) 
Maximum Building Coverage. The portion of the land area within the Master Plan 
PDA Area that is occupied by the footprint of buildings shall not exceed 50% in the 
aggregate, for purposes of which all buildings within the Master Plan PDA Area shall 
be taken into account, and compared against the entire land area of the Master Plan 
PDA Area including without limitation open space and roadways. In calculating the 
portion of land area that is occupied by the footprint of buildings, a building footprint 
shall not include areas located wholly below grade or below open space, roadways, 
courtyards, service areas, and/or other similar areas open to the sky. 
 
(ii) 
Active Uses. Designs for each building shall, to the extent possible, seek to maximize 
the storefront area used for Active Uses (as defined below) on building facades facing 
on Western Avenue and East, Cattle and Science Drives as determined through the 
BPDA design review process. As used in this Development Plan, “Active Uses” shall 
mean building lobbies, conference center uses and any of the following other uses if 
located on the ground floor: Restaurant Uses; Retail Uses; Hotel Uses; Facility of 
Public Assembly Uses; Neighborhood Medical Uses; Educational Uses, Art Uses; 
Entertainment Uses; Institutional Uses (as outlined and limited above); Community and 
Cultural Uses; and uses accessory thereto, in each case as outlined on Exhibit D. 
 
(iii) 
Parking, Service and Loading Dock Entrances; Private Service Driveways. For 
each building, dimensions and locations of curb cuts for parking entrances shall be 
determined through the BPDA design review process. 
 
(iv) 
Façade and Horizontal Building Wall Designs. Designs for each building, including 
horizontal facade massing, shall be determined through the BPDA design review 
process, as part of which buildings facades should be designed to maximize visual 
interest and avoid being perceived as a solid uninterrupted horizontal wall using 
publicly accessible ground-floor through-openings, or other such design features, or by 
being visually articulated as several smaller masses using different materials or colors, 
vertical breaks, bays, or other architectural elements. In addition, buildings should 
reflect a rhythm and variation appropriate to the urban context. 
 
 
Any variations from the use and dimensional requirements and urban design parameters set forth 
above and in Section 4 shall require approval pursuant to this Development Plan, and for material 
variations may also require an amendment to the Master Plan and this Development Plan, as 
determined by the BPDA.
